| **Remove from group** | Takes this task out of the group |
| **Edit group…**, **Archive group**, **Delete group…** | Act on the group itself, as from its header (below) |

**Group the list by your groups.** Turn on the **Your groups** switch in the **Group** menu. The line under the switch describes the result:

- **With None chosen** (*Shows a section per group*), each group is a section, in your own order whatever the sort, followed by **Ungrouped** for tasks without a group. Each group's archived tasks are in an **Archived** section just after the group, folded at first. A group with no tasks still has its section, so you can drop tasks into it.
- **With another grouping chosen** (*Shows {axis} within each group*), the control reads, for example, **Your groups › Inbox**, and each group has its own **Inbox** sections, which you can fold separately. On the **Board**, each group becomes a lane, and the grouping's sections become columns across every lane.

Until you have a group, the switch says *Drag a task onto another to group them*.

**A group's header.** Each group's header shows the group's color and name, then its count of active tasks and a dot for each state its tasks' sessions are in. A folded group therefore still shows whether something in it needs you. **Select** on a group header selects every task in the group. As the header gets narrower, it hides the session dots first, then shortens **Select** to an icon, so the name stays readable.

To open the group's menu, right-click the header or click its **⋮**. The menu acts on the group, never on its tasks:

| Item | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Edit group…** | Renames the group or changes its color, in the same form |
| **Change group color** | Picks one of the 8 colors directly |
| **Move group up**, **Move group down** | Moves the group one place in your order |
| **Archive group** | Archives the group. Offered only when every task in it is archived |
| **Delete group…** | Removes the group after a confirmation, *Its {count} tasks stay, ungrouped.* |

You can also drag a group's header to move the group before or after another group. **Ungrouped**, and the sections inside a group, cannot be moved.

**Archive or delete a group.** When a group's work is done and every task in it is archived, archive the group. The group disappears from every view, and you can reuse its name. If you restore one of its tasks, the group comes back too, and the task stays in it. Deleting a group never deletes its tasks. They stay where they are, without a group.

Agents can put tasks into groups too, through Kepler's workspace tools. See [What an agent can do with a task's resources](/kepler/tasks-and-resources#what-an-agent-can-do-with-a-tasks-resources).

### Fold a section

To fold or unfold a section, click its header. The header shows the section's count beside its name.

A folded section does not draw its rows, so a long **Done** list does not slow Kepler down. On the **Board** layout, a folded column shrinks to a narrow strip with its name and count, and is marked when it holds the open item. Click the strip to expand the column.

Some sections start folded:

- **Archived**, when you group by Activity or Inbox, because it holds work you have put away.
- **On hold**, in the Inbox grouping.

Under **Your groups**, folding a group hides the sections inside it, and you can fold each of those sections separately too.

Kepler remembers folds across restarts, for each segment and grouping. A section you folded stays folded, and a section you unfolded, such as **Archived**, stays open.

***

## Sort

The **Sort** control orders the items inside each section. It does not change the order of the sections, with 2 exceptions:

- **Repository** sections follow the sort, and each section's place depends on its first task.
- Your own groups always keep the order you gave them.

Each segment has its own sort options:

| Segment | Sort by | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **Todo** | Updated, Created, Name, ID, Type | Updated |
| **Tasks in progress** | Updated, Created, Name, Manual | Updated |

Dates sort newest first. **Name** and **ID** sort in ascending order. **ID** compares numbers by value, so *#9* comes before *#10*. **Type** puts pull requests before issues, with the most recent first within each. Each segment remembers its own sort.

### Put tasks in your own order

**Manual** sorts **Tasks in progress** in an order you set yourself, inside each section, in any grouping, on **List** or **Board**. To move a task, use one of these methods:

- Drag its row or card to a place in its own section. A line with a dot shows where it will land. Under **Manual**, a row shows a drag grip when you hover over it.
- Choose **Move up**, **Move down**, or **Move to top of {section}** from the task's **⋮** or right-click menu. These items appear only while the list is sorted by **Manual**.
- Drag one task of a selection to move all the selected tasks together. They land as one block, in the order they were listed. See [Act on several tasks at once](#act-on-several-tasks-at-once).

You do not have to switch to **Manual** first. If you drop a task in a new place in its own section while the list is sorted another way, Kepler saves the order you see, including your move, as the **Manual** order, and switches the sort to **Manual**. If you switch to **Manual** yourself, Kepler also keeps the current order, so no task changes place.

If you already have a saved **Manual** order, a drop under another sort would replace it. Kepler asks first, in a popover beside the dropped task: *Replace your Manual order?* To keep the move, choose **Switch and replace Manual**. To put the task back, choose **Cancel**, press **Escape**, or click away.

If a move fails, Kepler shows *Unable to move the task*, and restores the previous sort if the move had changed it.

***

## Set a task's progress

Kepler normally sets a task's progress stage from its Git branches and pull requests (see [Status](/kepler/kepler-interface)). Sometimes Git and the pull requests do not show what you know. For example, a review was sent back, or the work was merged somewhere Kepler cannot see. In those cases, set the stage yourself.

You can set the stage in these ways:

- **The progress control.** Click the stage name on a task row, in the preview header, or in the task page header to open the **Progress** menu: **Automatic** (*Updates as you work*), then **Exploration**, **In Development**, **In Review**, **On hold**, and **Done**. When there is no room for the stage name, the control shows only the stage's icon.
- **The task menus.** A task's **⋮** and right-click menus have the same choices under a **Progress** submenu, plus **Reopen** while the task is Done. Each item's hint says where the task will go (*Moves it to In Review*).
- **Drag a card.** In any grouping, on **List** or **Board**, drag a task's card or row. When grouped by **Progress**, drop it on another stage. On a touch screen, press and hold the card to pick it up. Press **Escape** to cancel the drag. If you drop the card in its own section, Kepler reorders it (see [Put tasks in your own order](#put-tasks-in-your-own-order)). You cannot drag a task that Kepler is still preparing. If you hold the card over another task, Kepler offers to group the 2 tasks (see [Your groups](#your-groups)). If you drag a task that is part of a selection, you drag the whole selection.
- **The Mark as bar.** While you drag, a **Mark as** bar appears over the toolbar with chips for what the card can become: **Read** or **Unread**, the stages, **Reopen** for a Done task, and **Archive task**. For an archived task, it shows only **Restore**. Drop the card on a chip.
- **From the keyboard.** When a card has focus on the **Board** grouped by **Progress**, press **Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+←** or **Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+→** to move it 1 column. The card stops at **Exploration** and **Done**.

While you drag, the card stays faded in its original place, and a line shows where it would land. Each section that accepts the card has a dashed outline, which becomes solid when the card is over it. Sections that do not accept the card fade, and say why when you hover over them. On the **Board**, a folded column opens after you hold the card over it for half a second.

The control's tooltip says whether the stage *Updates as you work* or was *Set manually*.

**How a stage you set works with Git.** Kepler keeps a stage you set until Git and the pull requests catch up with it or change. Then Kepler sets the stage from them again:

- If you set a stage *ahead* of Git and the pull requests (**Done** before the merge, or **In Review** before the pull request), the stage stays until they reach it.
- If you set a stage *behind* them (**Reopen**, or a review sent back to **In Development**), the stage stays until they change in any way. A reopened task therefore still follows its next pull request.
- To return the task to automatic stages sooner, choose **Automatic**, or drop its card on the column that Git and the pull requests already show.

**Reopen** on a task you marked Done returns it to the stage that Git and the pull requests show. If Git and the pull requests show the task as finished, **Reopen** sets **In Development**, and the task's next pull request moves it forward again.

**On hold** pauses a task without changing its stage. The task reads **On hold** where the stage would be, with a tooltip that says who put it on hold and what its stage was before. Choosing any stage or **Automatic** lifts the hold. The task reaching **Done** also lifts it, so a merged pull request ends the hold. You cannot put a task on hold when it is already at Done.

Dropping a card on **Archived** opens the archive confirmation. Dragging an archived card to another section restores the task first. An archived task's control reads **Archived** as a plain label, with no menu.

Agents can also set the stage, and put a task on hold, through Kepler's workspace tools. If an agent lifts a hold you placed, it tells you.

***

## Filter

The **Filter** menu has a submenu for each facet, such as **Progress** or **Provider**.

Kepler hides facets that have no values to choose from. For example, if you work in a single repository, the menu has no Repository facet. Each segment has these facets:

| Segment | Facets |
|---|---|
| **Todo** | Type · Linked work · Status · Needs my attention · Priority · Age · Your role · Provider, then one section per connected provider with its own Repository · Assignee · Issue type · Label · Project · Iteration or Sprint |
| **Tasks in progress** | Progress · Activity · Repository · Agent · Session · Linked work · Group |

**Issue type**, **Label**, **Project**, and **Iteration** use your provider's own values (a Jira issue type, your team's labels, a board name), not Kepler's own names for them. Azure DevOps calls the last one **Iteration** and Jira calls it **Sprint**, so the facet uses each tracker's word.

**Linked work** filters by whether an item is connected to work in the other segment:

- In Todo, it filters each pull request or issue by its task history: *Has an active task*, *Archived tasks only* (worked on before, but every task is archived), or *No tasks ever*.
- In Tasks in progress, it offers *Has a PR or issue*.

**Session** offers *Has a session* and *Has a live session*. To find tasks *without* a pull request, issue, or session, exclude the value.

**Group** lists each of [your groups](#your-groups), including empty ones, and **Ungrouped** for tasks without a group. If a filter still names a group that was deleted or archived, the facet shows it as **Removed group**. When the list is grouped by your groups, the facet also limits which group sections appear.

**Include or exclude any value.** Click a value to include it. To exclude a value instead, hover over it and click its minus button, or press **Shift+Enter** from the keyboard. An excluded value reads *not {value}*. On Todo, excluding a provider's value removes only that provider's items, so excluding a GitHub label never hides a Jira issue.

**Values you include in one facet are combined.** If you tick GitHub *and* GitLab under **Provider**, the list shows items from either provider. Excluded values remove items: Kepler hides an item that matches any of them. A facet with nothing chosen reads **Any** and does not narrow the list.

To find a facet value without scrolling, type in the **Search filters…** box. The menu shows **{count} of {total}** as you narrow the list. The **Filter** button names 1 chosen value and counts the rest, with included values in blue and excluded values in red.

To fetch the current segment from your providers again, click **Refresh**.

***

## Search

The search box finds items by **title, reference, or repository**. Its placeholder reads *Search title, ref, or repo…*.

When a search or a filter narrows the list, pills at the right end of the search box show how many rows are left or hidden. Each pill clears only its own search or filters:

| Pill | What it counts | Clicking it |
|---|---|---|
| The search pill | The rows on screen out of every row: *{count} of {total}* | Clears the search |
| The filter pill | The rows your filters hide: *{count} hidden* | Clears the filters |

While a search is on, the filter pill counts only hidden rows that match the search. If a search seems to miss something, the filter pill shows whether your filters are hiding it. Todo loads in pages, so its counts read *40+* or *7+ hidden* until everything has loaded.

When nothing matches, the empty list reads **Nothing matches your search**, or **Nothing matches these filters** when only filters narrow it. It offers a button named for what it resets: **Clear search**, **Clear filters**, or **Clear search and filters**.

Search covers only the work already loaded. On Todo, that is the work related to you on each connected integration, so when a search on Todo finds nothing, the list adds *Todo only searches work related to you.* To learn what each integration lists, see [Todo, Tasks in progress, and the Agent Graph](/kepler/kepler-interface#todo-tasks-in-progress-and-the-agent-graph).

***

## Saved views

To save a combination you use often, and return to it later, use the **Saved views** chip after the search box.

A view captures:

- The segment
- The search text
- The grouping, including whether **Your groups** is on
- The filters
- The layout (**List** or **Board**)

When you choose a view, Kepler restores all of these settings and switches to the view's segment. The chip then reads **View:** and the view's name, and a checkmark marks the view in the menu. Open preview panels are not part of a view, so applying a view never reopens a task or pull request that no longer exists.

The menu has these items:

| Menu item | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Save current view…** | Names the current combination and saves it as a new view |
| **Update saved view** | Overwrites the applied view with your edits. Available only after you change something |
| **Discard changes** | Puts the applied view back the way it was saved |
| **Rename view…** | Renames the applied view |
| **Delete view…** | Removes the applied view, after a confirmation |

A dot on the chip means you edited the applied view after you chose it. Every window shares the same views. Each view needs its own name, so Kepler adds a number to a duplicate name.

***

## What Kepler remembers

Each segment remembers its own search, grouping, sort, filters, layout, and folded sections, because the segments list different kinds of work. Kepler also remembers:

- **The segment you left**, which it restores along with that segment's settings.
- **Which panels were open**, until you quit Kepler. If you switch to the other segment and back, the panel you were reading is still open.
- **Panel widths**, for each window, across reloads and restarts.

Kepler does not remember the set of open panels across restarts, so a relaunch never opens a panel for a task that was deleted.

Saved views work differently from these per-segment settings. Kepler stores them by name and shares them across windows until you delete them.

***

## Archive, restore, and clean up in bulk

**Archive task** puts a task away. The task moves from its current section to **Archived**, its rows and sessions are kept, and Kepler stops only the agents whose checkout is about to be deleted.

When a task meets all of these conditions, the preview header and the task page header suggest archiving it, with *Ready to archive?* and an **Archive** button:

- The task is at **Done**.
- None of its worktrees has unpushed work.
- No agent is working or waiting on you.
- No session is running background work, such as a dev server.

**Archive** opens the usual confirmation. The **X** dismisses the suggestion for that task in every window.

The confirmation offers the same options as deleting a task: **Also delete worktrees**, **Also delete branches** (after you tick **Also delete worktrees**), and **Also delete the branch on the remote** (after you tick **Also delete branches**). You can therefore remove a finished task's worktrees and branches from disk without deleting the task. With **Also delete worktrees** ticked, the dialog lists each worktree, riskiest first, with what will happen to it (*Merged into main*, *2 uncommitted files*, *In open PR #42*). It also names the worktrees it keeps: the repository's main worktree, and worktrees that another task still uses. Kepler keeps a worktree that would lose work unless you tick the extra box that names exactly what would be lost. To check before you decide, open the changes from the row of a worktree at risk.

With **Also delete the branch on the remote** ticked, Kepler deletes each branch's remote copy after it deletes the local branch, unless a check says to keep it. Kepler keeps a branch with no upstream, or a default branch, without a message. For any other branch it keeps, a *Kept a branch on the remote* message says why, for example *it has an open pull request*, *it has commits that are not on the remote*, *the remote has commits this branch does not*, or *the remote branch changed after it was checked*.

**Archived** takes priority over every other section, so an archived task stays in **Archived** even if a shell is still open on it.

**Restore task** replaces **Archive task** in an archived task's **⋮** menu, and also appears in the task page's header. It restores the task at once, without asking, even when another active task holds the same pull request (several tasks can share one). A restored task stays in its group, and if that group was archived, Kepler restores the group too.

To archive, restore or delete several tasks at once, click **Select** on a section header in **Tasks in progress**. That part of the header becomes a bar with a select-all box, **{count} selected**, and icon buttons for the actions, each named in its tooltip. The section's rows show checkboxes. You can select in 1 section at a time, and while you select, clicking a row ticks it instead of opening its panel. A task that Kepler is still preparing has no checkbox, and select-all skips it.

The bar has these buttons:

| Button | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Archive** | Archives every selected task that is not already archived |
| **Restore** | Replaces **Archive** when every selected task is already archived |
| **Delete** | Deletes the selected tasks permanently |
| **Cancel** | Ends selection and clears the selection |

**Archive** and **Delete** both ask you to confirm, with **Archive tasks** or **Delete tasks** as the confirm button. Both offer **Also delete worktrees**, **Also delete branches**, and **Also delete the branch on the remote**. Deleting cannot be undone, and the confirmation says so. The batch confirmation differs from the single-task dialog in 2 ways:

- The single-task dialog remembers what you ticked last time. The batch confirmation always starts with all 3 boxes unticked.
- The batch confirmation does not list what will happen to each worktree. Instead, Kepler keeps any worktree that would lose work, and a message afterwards says which ones and why. To see the list before you confirm, use the task's own **⋮** menu.

### Act on several tasks at once

The tasks you open with **Shift**-click or **Cmd/Ctrl**-click (see [Open a panel](/kepler/kepler-interface#open-a-panel)) are also a selection you can act on. While 2 or more tasks are selected, right-clicking or dragging any one of them acts on all of them. Right-clicking or dragging a task outside the selection acts on that task only. A row's **⋮** always acts on its own row.

Right-clicking inside the selection opens a selection menu instead of the task menu. Each item shows how many tasks it acts on: **New group with {count} tasks…**, **Add {count} tasks to group**, **Remove {count} tasks from group**, **Archive {count} tasks**, **Restore {count} tasks**, and **Delete {count} tasks**. Kepler leaves out items with nothing to act on, and the group items skip archived tasks. While the menu is open, the rows it acts on are outlined. **Archive**, **Restore**, and **Delete** open the same batch confirmation as a section's **Select** bar.

Dragging a selected task drags the whole selection. Each drop target says how many of the tasks it accepts (*2 of 3 tasks*). After the drop, Kepler reports how many tasks moved and how many stayed where they were. Under the **Manual** sort, the tasks land together as one block.

To clean up worktrees and local branches instead of tasks, open **Settings → Repositories** and choose **Manage worktrees and branches**. The **Worktrees and branches** page lists every worktree, and every local branch that no worktree has checked out. You can filter the list by **Safe to delete**, **Needs update**, **Conflicts**, **Stale**, or **All**. On this page, you can:

- **Update** several worktrees at once, which brings each branch up to date with its base.
- Delete worktrees and branches, including their copies on the remote.

See [Settings](/kepler/settings-repositories#worktrees-and-branches).

---

---
# Actions
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/actions/
product: Kepler
feature: Actions
content_type: how-to
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-10

An **Action** is a named prompt you fire at a task, issue, or pull request to start agent work.

Every Action is yours to configure. You pick the wording, you pick the agent, and you pick which Action is the one-click default for each kind of work.

***

## The four built-in Actions

Kepler ships with four Actions. Every one of them is editable.

| Action | What it asks the agent to do | Offered on |
|---|---|---|
| **Plan** | Research the code first, write out the proposed approach, change nothing, and wait for your confirmation | Tasks, Issues, Pull requests |
| **Implement** | Read enough surrounding code to be confident, then make the changes directly rather than describing them | Tasks, Issues, Pull requests |
| **Review** | Review the pull request if one is attached, otherwise the uncommitted work in the worktree | Tasks, Pull requests |
| **Address Feedback** | Triage the review comments, apply what's worth applying, and push back on the rest instead of applying every suggestion blindly | Pull requests |

**Kepler deliberately offers Review on plain tasks.** Reviewing your own uncommitted work before you push is the obvious thing to want from a worktree. One flexible Review covers both cases, rather than splitting the list into "review a pull request" and "review my changes."

Every Action declares **what it can be aimed at**, which is why **Address Feedback** never appears on a task with no pull request.

You can edit and reset built-in Actions, but you can't delete them. What an Action applies to already controls where it shows up, so deleting one would be a weaker version of the same control.

***

## Where the Action button appears

You fire Actions from a **split button**. The left half runs your preferred Action for that surface; the chevron opens the full list.

<div class="table-center" markdown="1">

| Surface | Preferred Action comes from |
|---|---|
| A row in **Todo** (an issue or pull request) | the row's own kind of item |
| The side panel, on the selected item | the selected item's kind |

</div>

Firing an Action from a Todo row is also how an issue or pull request that isn't tracked yet **becomes** a task in Kepler.

On a Todo row, the button rests as a quiet outline and fills in only while you hover or select its row, so a column of buttons doesn't compete with the rows. On a narrow card it shrinks to a play icon. On a phone, a row has a single **⋮** menu instead (**Actions for {title}**) that lists every Action, the preferred one included, and the side panel has no Action button.

In the list of Actions, hover a row, or move focus to it, to read that Action's prompt, line breaks included.

Inside a task, Actions live under the **chevron on the composer's send button** rather than on a split button of their own: type a refinement, then pick the Action to fire it with. In a composer that starts something new, such as the **New task** composer or a panel's draft, picking an Action doesn't fire it: it sets the main button to that Action, and shows the Action's own agent in the agent pill if it names one, so you can check what will run before you press it. See [Create a task](/kepler/create-task#from-the-new-task-composer).

Task rows don't carry an Action button. A task's own operations live behind the **⋮** menu on the row instead.

A task row has no **Resume** button. Clicking the row selects it and shows its sessions, the way to look at running work without sending anything. Firing an Action on live work takes you to the session that Action landed in instead.

***

## Firing an Action

An Action fires immediately unless Kepler is unclear on where to run the action.

### The left half: one click

The left half of the button runs your preferred Action straight away, in the current session if one exists. It only stops to ask when the task has **two or more worktrees**.

The number of issues or pull requests attached to the task doesn't change what the Action does. An Action's prompt is its own content, word for word, and every attached item ships to the agent as shared context. All of it is the work. If you want the agent to look at one thing first, say so in the prompt box or in the chat; that's one sentence, and it's better in your own words.

### The chevron: the deliberate path

Picking an Action from the chevron list always goes on to ask where to run it, whenever there is anything at all to choose, including new-session-vs-current on a task with a single worktree, which the left half answers silently.

At the bottom of the list, **Manage Actions…** opens **Settings → Actions**.

From the keyboard, the two halves are separate **Tab** stops, the Action first. **Down Arrow** or **Alt+Down** on the Action opens the list too, and closing the list puts focus back on the Action. Every split button in Kepler (**Send**, **Open in**, **Run**) works the same way.

### Choosing where it runs

The **Run in** view asks two independent questions, and both have small answers.

**New session, or a current one?** A two-way toggle between **New session** and **Current session**. *Current session* lists every reusable session with its worktree, so clicking a row queues the Action into that exact session.

**Which worktree?** In *New session*, the rows are **All N worktrees**, **A new worktree**, and then one row per branch. In *Current session*, individual sessions replace branches that already have sessions.

Clicking any row **runs the Action** immediately, with no separate confirm step.

Two things worth knowing:

- **A worktree with no session open still runs** under *Current session*. It starts one there, so *all worktrees* always means all of them.
- **Kepler navigates to the first destination you picked**, not to whichever session happened to start first.

Worktree choices are resolved against worktrees that actually exist on disk, so a task that still names a worktree you've since removed won't silently run somewhere else.

A task with no worktree runs the Action in a folder attached to it, or else in the task's own folder. With neither, Kepler says *This task has no folder or worktree to start a session in.*

### Firing into a running session

Firing into a live session **queues** the prompt behind whatever the agent is currently doing. Nothing is dropped and nothing is canceled, and Kepler takes you to the session the prompt went into.

***

## Set your preferred Actions

To set your preferred Actions, open **Settings → Actions → Preferred Actions**.

Each row sets the Action that the left half of the button runs for that kind of item.

<div class="table-center" markdown="1">

| Setting | Default |
|---|---|
| **Tasks** | Implement |
| **Issues** | Plan |
| **Pull requests I authored** | Address Feedback |
| **Pull requests from others** | Review |

</div>

Pull requests split by **who wrote them**, not by what you want to do with them. Kepler works out review-vs-address-feedback from authorship, so the settings name the *kind of pull request* rather than the intent. When you want the other one, it's one click away in the chevron.

Any slot can be set to **None**. This simplifies the action button to only display the chevron icon.

***

## Edit an Action

To edit an Action, go to **Settings → Actions** and click the Action's row under **All Actions**. The editor opens as its own page.

Once you have a custom Action, the list splits into **Built in** and **Custom**. Until then, it shows the built-in Actions without labels.

The editor has these fields:

| Field | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Title** | The name shown on the button and in the chevron list. Required: *Title can't be empty.* |
| **Prompt** | Sent to the agent word for word. It *Can be, or start with, one of your skills*: type **/** (or **$** for Codex) to pick one. Required: *Prompt can't be empty.* |
| **Applies to** | **Tasks**, **Issues**, **Pull requests**: controls where the Action is offered. Pick at least one |
| **Agent** | Which agent runs it. See below |

### Create your own

To create an Action, click **New Action** in **Settings → Actions**.

Custom Actions work exactly like the built-in ones, and they're the point of the feature: if you'd do something more than once (backport a fix, write the migration, audit a dependency bump), it should be a button rather than a prompt you retype.

#### Example: Prepare for review

This Action asks the agent to gather the evidence a reviewer needs before you read the diff, so you start from what the agent did and what it didn't check. To create it, click **New Action** in **Settings → Actions** and fill in the following fields:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **Title** | Prepare for review |
| **Applies to** | **Tasks** |
| **Agent** | Inherit, or a different agent from the one that wrote the code |

Use the following text for **Prompt**:

```text
Before I review this work, write a review summary in this session. Include:
- What the change is supposed to do, in one or two sentences
- Each file you changed, and why
- The commands you ran to test the change, and their results
- What you didn't test, and anything you're unsure about
Don't change any files.
```

The summary is the agent's own account. Check it against the diff in [Review Changes](/kepler/review-changes) before you commit.

#### Example: Open a pull request

Kepler has no "create pull request" button, so the agent or you open one. This Action has the agent open it, with a note in the description that an agent helped write the change. Fire it after you've reviewed and committed the work. To create it, click **New Action** in **Settings → Actions** and fill in the following fields:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| **Title** | Open a pull request |
| **Applies to** | **Tasks** |
| **Agent** | Inherit |

Use the following text for **Prompt**:

```text
Push this worktree's branch and open a pull request against its base branch.
Write a title and a description that say what changed and why.
End the description with this line:
"An AI coding agent helped write this change, and a person reviewed it."
If the worktree has uncommitted changes, stop and tell me.
```

The agent opens the pull request with the tools it has, such as your Git host's command-line tool. When it publishes the pull request, Kepler attaches it to the task. See [Review Changes](/kepler/review-changes#opening-a-pull-request).

### Restore defaults

To undo your edits to one Action, click **Restore default** on its row. The row shows **Restore default** only after you edit the Action. To undo your edits to every Action at once, click **Restore all defaults** in the **All Actions** section header.

Kepler stores **only what you changed**, not a copy of the whole Action. This creates the following considerations when restoring defaults:

- An Action you've never edited picks up improved wording in a future Kepler release.
- **Restore default** works by forgetting your edit. Editing an Action back to its original wording has the same effect.

Deleting a custom Action that a preferred-Action slot points to is the same as setting it to **None**. You will see rows with only the chevron, instead of the preferred-Action + the chevron. Revisit the Actions setting to set a new preference.

***

## Setting an Action's agent

By default an Action runs on your **default agent**, configured in **Settings → Tasks → New tasks → Default agent**. The **Agent** field in the Action editor reads **Inherit** until you name one.

Naming an agent is an **all-or-nothing override**: it pins the provider, account, model, mode, and options together, rather than changing one of them and inheriting the rest. This is what makes per-Action cost tuning work: a cheap, fast model for triage and review, a heavier one for implementation.

Three rules govern which agent actually runs:

- A model belongs to its provider, so a pinned model never runs on a different agent.
- If an Action names an agent you don't have installed, the override falls back **whole** to your default agent.
- **An agent you pick explicitly at the point of firing beats an Action's override.**

### Review with a different agent

You can have one agent write the code and a different agent review it. A reviewer that didn't write the code is less likely to repeat the author's mistakes.

To give **Review** its own agent, take the following steps:

1. Go to **Settings → Actions**, and click **Review** under **All Actions**.
2. Name a different agent in the **Agent** field from the one that writes your code. **Implement** uses your default agent unless you've changed it.
3. Click **Save**.

**Review** now runs on that agent, whether you fire it at a task's uncommitted work or at an attached pull request. The override is all-or-nothing, so it also pins that agent's account, model, and mode.

To use a different reviewer just once, pick the agent when you fire **Review**. An agent you pick at that point beats the Action's override.

The review is a report, not an approval. You read it in the session and decide what to change before you commit.

---

---
# Tasks and Resources
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/tasks-and-resources/
product: Kepler
feature: Tasks
content_type: concept
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-10

A **task** is the unit of work in Kepler. It is one thing you want to get done, plus everything the agents working on it need: the repositories, the issue or pull request it came from, the branches, the notes, and every agent session you have run on it.

You can start a task with as much or as little as you have:

- Start a task from an issue in [the Kepler interface](/kepler/kepler-interface), and it opens with the repository and the issue body already attached.
- Start a task with nothing attached (no repository, no branch) to explore an idea, and attach the repositories and issues later.

***

## What a task holds

Everything attached to a task is a **resource**.

To attach a resource, use one of these controls on the task page:

- **Add resource**, at the bottom of the context panel, opens a dialog titled **Add to this task**. Its tabs cover every kind of resource: **Repos & Folders**, **Issues**, **Pull requests**, **Notes**, **Links** and **Files**.
- The **+** on a group header in the context panel opens the same dialog for that kind of resource only. Its title names the kind, such as **Add a note** or **Add a link**.

A task can hold these kinds of resource:

| Resource | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Sessions** | Agent conversations that run on this task |
| **Terminals** | Shells opened in one of the task's working directories |
| **Worktrees** | Git working copies that the agents change. The context panel lists them under **Changes**, because you go there to read the changes |
| **Folders** | A directory that is not a Git repository. The agent works on it in place |
| **Files** | A single file, when you need the file rather than its whole folder. A file is either linked from disk by its path or uploaded to the task as a copy |
| **Pull requests** | Pull requests from your connected Git hosts |
| **Issues** | Issues from your connected trackers |
| **Links** | Any URL you want to keep with the work |
| **Notes** | Text you write, such as standing instructions, decisions and reference material. The task's own **Prompt** is the first item in this group |

A task can hold **more than one** of each kind. For example, a task can span 3 repositories and link 2 issues.

To learn how the task page is laid out (the context panel, columns, split panes and tabs), see [the task page](/kepler/task-view).

### Picking issues and pull requests

The **Issues** and **Pull requests** tabs list work from your connected providers, under a search field and a row of filters. Each row shows the item's title, a line with its identifier, repository and provider, and its age.

To see more about an item before you add it, click **Show preview** beside the search field, or press **Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+P**. The list splits to show a preview of the focused item: its repository, author, labels and description. Kepler remembers this choice on this computer. A narrow dialog does not offer the preview, because the preview needs the room.

You can use the list from the keyboard:

| Key | What it does |
|---|---|
| **↓** from the search field | Moves into the list |
| **↑** / **↓**, **Home** / **End** | Moves between rows |
| **Space** | Selects or clears the focused row |
| **Enter** | Adds what you selected, or the focused row when nothing is selected |

To add a single item, double-click its row. The main button shows how many items you selected, as in **Add to task · 1**. To add the selection and keep the dialog open, click **Add & keep adding**.

### Pasting an issue link

The **Links** tab accepts any URL. When you paste an issue's URL, Kepler looks up the issue (*Looking up issue…*) before you can add it. If Kepler finds the issue, the field reads *Adds {provider} issue {key}: {title}*, and Kepler adds the link as that issue, under the issue's title, rather than as a plain link. To add it as a plain link anyway, click **Add as plain link**.

If the lookup finds nothing, or cannot reach the provider, Kepler shows one of these messages and adds a plain link instead:

- *No issue found for that link. It may not exist or you may not have access; it will be added as a plain link.*
- *Unable to look up that issue. It will be added as a plain link.*

### Files: linked or uploaded

The **Files** group holds 2 kinds of file. Kepler removes them differently, because it owns only the uploaded copy:

| Kind | Where it lives | Its row reads | Removing it |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Linked file** | Where it already was on disk. Kepler links to it by its path and never changes it | Its path | **Detach file…** leaves the file where it is |
| **Uploaded copy** | In the task's own folder. It belongs to this task only | **Task folder** | **Delete file…** deletes the copy |

Other ways files reach a task:

- When you attach a file to a prompt, Kepler copies it into the task when you send the prompt. That copy is an uploaded copy too.
- In a window connected to another machine, the file picker on the **Files** tab of **Add resources** also offers **Upload from this machine**. It copies files from the machine you are using into the task's folder.

To save either kind of file somewhere else, choose **Save as…** from its menu.

### Issues and pull requests attach themselves

You do not have to attach a task's pull request yourself. If a task holds no pull request yet, and one of its worktrees is on a branch that exactly matches an open pull request's head branch, Kepler attaches that pull request to the task. This works however the pull request was opened, including from a terminal, from GitKraken, or on the web.

Kepler limits automatic attachment to these cases, because a wrong match would put someone else's work into your agent's context:

- The branch names must match exactly. A similar name does not match.
- Kepler attaches only open pull requests whose head branch is in the same repository. A pull request from a fork is never attached automatically.
- Kepler attaches a pull request even when another active task already holds it. Several tasks can share 1 pull request, and attaching it to one task never archives it or detaches it from the other.

**Issues attach the same way.** When an issue's branch matches one of the task's checkouts, Kepler attaches the issue. A task you start from a branch name therefore gets the issue behind that branch.

Automatic attachment only adds links. It never removes one. To remove a link you do not want on the task, detach it.

**Work item URLs attach as issues.** When you or an agent attaches one of the following URLs, Kepler records it as an issue rather than a plain link:

- A GitLab work item, such as `https://gitlab.com/{group}/{project}/-/work_items/{number}`
- An Azure DevOps work item, such as `https://dev.azure.com/{organization}/{project}/_workitems/edit/{id}`, or the organization-level `https://dev.azure.com/{organization}/_workitems/edit/{id}`

A GitLab work item that belongs to a group rather than a project stays a plain link.

### Keeping them current

Kepler refreshes a task's pull requests and issues when something happens that could change them:

- An agent ends a turn.
- Someone pushes one of the task's branches.
- Someone publishes a pull request.

Kepler re-reads only that task, so a busy task does not trigger a refresh of your whole account. Kepler looks up each link where it lives: in the repository it names, or on the Jira site or Linear workspace in its URL. As a result, 2 repositories with the same issue number, or 2 Jira sites with the same key, stay separate.

A Jira or Linear issue that moves to a new key stays attached under the link you added, and Kepler keeps refreshing it from that link.

To refresh by hand, click the refresh button on the **Pull requests** or **Issues** group header, or choose **Refresh** in the task's **⋮** menu. A refresh you ask for re-reads the provider instead of showing what Kepler already had. It re-reads every stored link in full, including merged pull requests.

***

## Worktrees and working in place

A **worktree** is a private Git working copy for one task. Agents make their changes in the worktree, so nothing they do touches the checkout you work in, and several agents can run at once without changing each other's files. Use a worktree for most work.

When you add a repository to a task through **Add resource**, the **Isolated worktree** toggle sets whether the task gets a worktree. When you create a task, the repository chip in the **New task** composer offers the same choice through a different control, which adds a branch-name field. See [Create a task](/kepler/create-task#configuring-a-repository).

| Setting | What it says |
|---|---|
| **On** | *Its own folder. Nothing else can switch its branch.* |
| **Off** | *Uses your repository folder. Anything that switches its branch switches it here too.* |

If the branch you picked is already checked out somewhere, Git cannot check it out a second time. The toggle locks and says where the task will work instead: *Uses {worktree}, which already has this branch.* or *Uses your repository folder, which already has this branch.* With isolation off, the picker reads **directly in repo**.

> **With isolation off, the task has no branch of its own.** The task uses your repository folder exactly as it is. Kepler copies nothing and protects nothing. Turn isolation off only when you want an agent to work in your own checkout. Otherwise, leave it on.

Kepler always isolates a repository linked to a pull request, and locks the toggle: *This repository is linked to a pull request and always opens in its own isolated working copy.*

When you attach the repository, you can also pick the branch:

- **Use this branch** works directly on an existing branch.
- **New branch** creates a branch from the repository's default branch.

Each option says where the work will happen, such as *Branch off {branch} in a new worktree*. Kepler names a new branch for you unless you set a name. Kepler reads the branch list again each time you open it, and **Refresh branches**, beside **Find a branch…**, fetches from your remotes first.

**A new branch starts from the repository's remote default branch**, not from the branch you have checked out. To start from another branch, name a base yourself:

- A local base starts from its upstream.
- If the local base has commits you have not pushed, the new branch starts from your local tip instead, so it includes those commits.

If Kepler cannot resolve a remote default branch (no remote, a shallow clone, or offline with nothing cached), it starts the branch from the current HEAD instead of refusing to start.

Kepler suggests branch names from the task's own context. A suggested name starts with the issue identifier when the task has one, and sits under the `kepler/` prefix unless you configure another prefix. See [Create a task](/kepler/create-task#naming-the-branch).

**A task does not require a worktree, or even a repository.** Attach a plain folder, and the agent works on it in place. Attach nothing, and you have a space to explore an idea. You can attach repositories and other resources later, when you are ready to start the work.

### When a worktree goes missing

A worktree deleted outside Kepler **stays bound to its task**, so the task keeps its record of where the work was, even after a `git worktree prune`. The row is flagged **Gone from disk**, and the pane shows the details Kepler recorded: **Current branch**, **Base branch**, and **Recorded path**.

To bring the worktree back, click **Recreate worktree** on the pane, or choose it from the worktree's menu. Kepler recreates the worktree at the recorded path. If the branch was deleted too, Kepler rebuilds it in this order:

1. If the branch's last commit still exists in the repository, Kepler restores the branch at that commit, with its history.
2. Otherwise, Kepler creates the branch again from the recorded base branch.
3. If the base branch is gone too, as it usually is after its pull request merges, Kepler creates the branch from the repository's default branch.

Kepler tells you which branch it started from. Recreating one worktree clears only that worktree's stale Git entry. Other missing worktrees, such as ones on an unplugged drive, keep their entries.

An attached folder that was removed stays on the task the same way. If you start a new session in a worktree or folder that is gone, Kepler asks first (*Recreate the worktree and start the session?*). It then rebuilds the worktree or folder before the session starts, so the agent never starts in a directory that does not exist. A task with no repository or folder starts its sessions in the task's own folder.

### Make a new worktree ready to build

A new worktree is a clean checkout. It has no `node_modules`, no build output, and none of the files your setup script would normally create. An agent that starts there has to install dependencies first, or its first build fails.

To prepare new worktrees automatically, use **Commands**. Save a repository's setup steps once, such as `pnpm install` or a code generation step, and tick **Run on worktree creation**. Each time Kepler creates a worktree for that repository, it runs those commands in order in the new worktree's folder, before the agent starts. To run a command that is not set to run on creation, right-click a worktree in the context panel and choose **Run command here**.

The worktree's menu has the same entries wherever the worktree appears:

- **Run command here**, **New session here**, which opens a draft session in that worktree, and **New terminal here**.
- The **Branch** submenu, with **Rename branch**, the upstream, **Change merge target…**, and **Rebase onto {target}** or **Merge {target} into this branch**. For the upstream and updating the branch, see [Review Changes](/kepler/review-changes#publishing-and-syncing-the-branch).
- The copy actions, **Refresh**, **Detach worktree…** and **Delete worktree…**.

To set up commands, open **Settings → Repositories** and go to the repository's own page. See [Settings](/kepler/settings-repositories#per-repository-commands) for the fields, the **Variables** a command can use, and what happens when one fails.

### What a worktree does not separate

A worktree gives each task its own copy of the files, but nothing else. Tasks still share everything outside the worktree's folder:

- **Ports.** Two worktrees that start the same dev server on the same port collide, and the second server fails to start.
- **Databases and other local services.** Agents in different worktrees that point at the same database read and write the same data.
- **Caches and files outside the repository.** A global package cache or a file in your home folder is the same for every worktree.

To keep tasks apart, give each worktree its own settings when Kepler creates it. Add a per-repository command that runs on worktree creation and writes those settings, such as a port or a database name, into a local config file in the new worktree. The command runs in the new worktree's folder, and its **Variables** menu can insert the worktree's path. See [Settings](/kepler/settings-repositories#per-repository-commands).

***

## Shared context: how resources reach your agents

Kepler sends everything attached to a task to **every agent session in the task** as *shared context*: the task's prompt, the issue body, the pull request, your notes and the links. When a prompt refers to something *"described in the shared context above"*, it means these items.

Kepler sends each kind of item differently:

- **The task's prompt** goes in full, as background to the work rather than as an instruction. The agent acts on the messages you send it.
- **Each note** goes as a reference, with its title and size. The agent reads the note's text through Kepler's Model Context Protocol (MCP) server when it needs it. A session that cannot reach that server gets the full text of every note instead.

**Launching a task saves its issues' descriptions as notes.** When you launch a task with linked issues, Kepler reads each issue again and saves its description as a note titled *Issue {identifier}: {title}*, with the issue's URL at the top. Each description is limited to 8 KB, and all of them together to 16 KB. Kepler cuts a longer description short and adds a pointer to the URL. Kepler tells agents that the text comes from a third party, so they treat it as information rather than instructions.

In the conversation, shared context appears as a collapsible row with a count of the items included. The row reads **Task context added** the first time, and **Task context updated** each time the context changes. Expand the row to see exactly what the agent received.

You do not edit shared context directly. To change it, attach, detach or edit resources. Each session receives the change with its next prompt, so the change does not interrupt an agent during a turn.

### The task's prompt is context too

The text you wrote when you started the task is a context item of its own: the **Prompt**, at the top of the **Notes** group. Every session on the task works toward this prompt, so Kepler sends it with the rest of the shared context. When the goal changes, edit the prompt the same way you edit a note. Unlike a note, the prompt cannot be deleted.

### Starting a session without the task's context

Sometimes you want an agent that forms its own view, such as a reviewer that should not be influenced by the implementer's brief. To start a session without the task's prompt and notes, follow these steps:

1. Click **+** on the **Sessions** group in the context panel, or press **Cmd/Ctrl+T**. A draft session tab opens.
2. In the draft's composer footer, untick the **Task context** chip. The chip is on by default, and its tooltip reads *Gives the agent the task’s prompt and notes. Later changes reach it with your next message.*
3. Type your prompt and click **Start**.

The new session does not receive the task's prompt or notes. It still gets the task's worktrees, folders, files and links, because it still needs to know where to work. The chip applies only to that draft, so turning it off does not change your other sessions. See [Starting a session](/kepler/task-view#starting-a-session).

### Notes are how you give standing instructions

Attach a **Note** for anything every agent on the task should follow, such as a style rule, a constraint, or a decision you do not want reopened. Write it once, and every session gets it, including sessions you start later. A session sees a note's title first and opens the note when it is relevant, so give each note a title that says what it covers. A note can be up to 1 MB. Kepler refuses a longer note with *This note is too long. Notes can be up to 1 MB.*

To rename a note, double-click its name, press **F2** on the open note, or choose **Rename note** from its right-click menu. The name becomes a field. Press **Enter** to keep the new name, or **Escape** to restore the old one. A note with no name reads **Untitled note**. The task's **Prompt** cannot be renamed.

To edit an open note, click **Edit**, or press **Enter** on the focused note. **Copy note**, beside **Edit**, copies the note. If you leave an edit unsaved, Kepler keeps it as a draft: the note reads **Unsaved draft**, and **Edit** becomes **Resume draft**.

***

## Detaching and deleting

Removing a resource from a task usually leaves the resource itself intact. The menu shows which action you are taking:

- **Detach** removes something that lives elsewhere, such as a folder or a pull request, from the task.
- **Delete** removes something that only the task holds, such as a note or an uploaded copy.

Each kind of resource has its own confirmation dialog, because removing it has a different effect:

| Resource | Dialog | What removing it does |
|---|---|---|
| **Folder** | *Detach folder?* | *The folder stays on disk — it's only removed from this task.* |
| **Linked file** | *Detach file?* | *The file stays on disk — it's only removed from this task.* |
| **Uploaded copy** | *Delete file?* | *Deletes the copy in the task folder.* |
| **Pull request** or **issue** | *Detach pull request?* / *Detach issue?* | *It's removed from this task.* |
| **Link** | *Delete link?* | *It's removed from this task.* |
| **Note** | *Delete note?* | *Deletes the note.* |

The task's **Prompt** has no remove action.

Deleting a worktree can lose work, so Kepler adds more checks before it deletes one.

The worktree's menu, in the context panel or in the worktree tab's header, has 2 separate entries:

- **Detach worktree…** removes the worktree from the task and leaves it on disk. Its dialog says only *The worktree stays on disk — it’s only removed from this task.*
- **Delete worktree…** removes the worktree from disk. It opens **Delete worktree?**, which warns *This can’t be undone.* when confirming would delete something. The repository's main worktree has no **Delete worktree…** entry.

The **Delete worktree?** dialog lists the worktree with what deleting it would cost, such as **No uncommitted changes** and **Branch kept**, under a verdict such as **Safe to delete**. To remove the branch along with the worktree, tick **Also delete branch**. You cannot delete a worktree that another task still uses. In that case, the dialog names the task that uses it and offers **Detach worktree** instead of **Delete worktree**.

You cannot detach or delete a worktree while a session is still running in it. The menu tells you how many sessions to archive first. If another program has the folder open, the delete fails with *Kepler could not delete {path} because another program is using it. Close any editors, terminals or file explorers that have the folder open, then try again.*

Below the worktree, a live check shows what deleting would cost. Kepler reads this from the worktree when the dialog opens. When you tick **Also delete branch**, the check runs again, because deleting the branch can lose different work. Each worktree has short tags that show what you could lose:

| Tag | What it means |
|---|---|
| *{count} uncommitted files* | Changes that exist only in this working copy |
| *{count} commits not on any remote* | Commits on the branch that were never pushed. Kepler counts them before it deletes anything |
| *Detached HEAD* | Commits that are not on any branch |
| *In open PR #{prNumber}*, *Merged in PR #{prNumber}*, *Merged into {base}*, *Pushed* | The branch's commits are stored somewhere else, so deleting the branch loses nothing |
| *No uncommitted changes* | Nothing to lose |

Kepler treats a branch that was merged through a rebase merge or a squash merge as merged. When you clean up such a branch, Kepler does not warn about commits that are already in its target.

Kepler **keeps** a worktree that would lose work, unless you tick the extra box that names the worktree and what it would lose: *Also delete {branch}, losing {what}*. Without that confirmation, Kepler refuses the delete. Whatever requests the delete, Kepler never deletes uncommitted or unpushed work without your confirmation.

***

## Renaming, archiving, and deleting a task

To rename, archive or delete a task, open the **Task actions** (**⋮**) menu on the task's row or in the task page's header. The menu has these actions:

| Action | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Mark as read** / **Mark as unread** | **Mark as read** appears while any of the task's sessions is unread, and marks them all read. Otherwise the menu offers **Mark as unread** |
| **Rename task** | Turns the name, which Kepler set when you created the task, into a field (on the task page, double-clicking the name does the same). **Auto-name** puts a suggestion based on the task's prompt and resources into the field, for you to accept or edit |
| **Add to group** | Puts the task in one of [your groups](/kepler/arranging-your-work#your-groups), starts a **New group…** with it, or offers **Remove from group** when the task is in a group. A task with sub-tasks also offers **Group with its {count} sub-tasks**, and an archived task does not offer **Add to group** |
| **Copy task link** | Copies a Kepler link to the task. **Cmd/Ctrl+C** on a focused task row also copies it |
| **Refresh** | Reads the task's worktrees and its pull request and issue links again. For a short time after a refresh, Kepler cannot read the providers again, so the row is locked and says when you can try again |
| **Archive task** | Removes the task from the active list and keeps it as history. Kepler keeps its sessions and resources, and deletes nothing unless you ask it to |
| **Restore task** | Replaces **Archive task** on an archived task, and returns it to the active list, even when another active task holds the same pull request (several tasks can share one). The task stays in its group, and restores the group too if the group was archived |
| **Delete task** | Removes the task along with its sessions and resources |

**Kepler suggests archiving a finished task.** When a task meets all of these conditions, its header asks *Ready to archive?* with an **Archive** button:

- The task is at **Done**.
- Its worktrees have no unpushed work.
- No session is still working, waiting on you, or running background work.

If you dismiss the suggestion, Kepler stops suggesting it for that task.

**Archive** and **Delete** open the same dialog, with the same 3 checkboxes for the task's worktrees and branches. Each box stays unavailable until you tick the one above it, and Kepler remembers your choices for next time:

- **Also delete worktrees**
- **Also delete branches**
- **Also delete the branch on the remote**

Until you tick a box, the dialog reads *Worktrees and branches stay on disk unless you tick the boxes below.* When you tick **Also delete worktrees**, Kepler lists every worktree with the same tags that a single worktree delete shows, and says what will happen to each:

- Kepler deletes a worktree that is safe to delete.
- Kepler **keeps** a worktree that would lose work, *because deleting it would lose work*, unless you tick the box that names the worktree and confirms the loss.
- Kepler lists a worktree it cannot delete with the reason: another task still uses it, it is the repository's main worktree, a session still runs in it, or it is already gone from disk.

When you tick **Also delete branches**, Kepler checks the list again, so a worktree that was safe can now show a warning. If the check is slow, you can confirm anyway. Kepler still keeps any worktree that would lose work.

When **Also delete the branch on the remote** is ticked, Kepler deletes each branch's remote copy after it deletes the local branch. Kepler keeps the remote branch if deleting it could lose something, and a *Kept a branch on the remote* notice gives the reason:

- The branch has an open pull request.
- The branch has commits that are not on the remote.
- The remote has commits that this branch does not have.
- The remote branch changed after Kepler checked it.

**Restore task** appears in the task page's header as soon as you archive the task. On a row in the main list, it appears only after you filter **Activity** to **Archived**. See [Arranging Your Work](/kepler/arranging-your-work).

To archive or restore a single session, use the session's own menu in the context panel.

***

## What an agent can do with a task's resources

Agents work with tasks through Kepler's own MCP server, `kepler-workspace`. With its tools, an agent can keep the task's resources up to date for you, and can find and coordinate with the rest of your work.

<div class="note" markdown="1">

**The workspace tools were renamed in Kepler 0.15.** Each tool is now named for what it acts on, then what it does, such as `task_get` or `worktree_create`. If an agent's settings allow-list `mcp__kepler-workspace__` tools by name, update them to the names below.

</div>

The tools refer to things by id, and each id starts with its kind: `task:`, `session:`, `repo:`, `worktree:`, `folder:`, `note:`, `file:`, `account:`, `group:` and `comment:`. If you paste a Kepler link to a task or a session into the chat, the agent can use it as the id. Wherever a tool takes a repository, the agent can also name the repository by one of its **Aliases**, which you set on the repository's page in **Settings → Repositories**. See [Settings](/kepler/settings-repositories#edit-a-repository).

**Reading tasks and notes**

| Tool | What it does |
|---|---|
| `task_get` | Read a task: its stage, group, worktrees and folders, notes, files, links, related tasks, newest sessions, and how many of your review comments are still open. On the agent's own task, later calls return only what changed, and `refresh` first reads the pull request and issue state, the disk and Git again |
| `task_list` | Find tasks by name, prompt, note text or file name, filtered by stage, hold, repository, [group](/kepler/arranging-your-work#your-groups), or whether they belong to the agent's own work. Each task shows its group, the first page lists every group you have, including empty ones, and archived tasks appear only on request |
| `task_note_read` | Read one note's full text. Otherwise, notes arrive as references (title and size) |
| `task_comment_read` | Read the open [review comments](/kepler/review-changes#review-comments) you sent on a task's code (those still waiting on an agent's answer first, each with its file, lines, the code it is on, and its replies), or read one comment by id, resolved or not. Comments you have not sent cannot be read |

**Finding sessions, agents and places**

| Tool | What it does |
|---|---|
| `session_list` | Find agent sessions by name, task, agent or place, with each session's state and what it is waiting on: a permission, an answer, or an approval. It can list only the sessions that need you |
| `session_read` | Read another session's conversation, at the level of detail the agent asks for, by its id or a link from **Copy session link**. It returns the newest messages, or only the last reply with `limit:1`, and reports what a running session waits on, including a plan it is holding for your review |
| `agent_list` | List the agents, accounts, models and effort values a new session can start with, and the modes each agent supports |
| `repo_list` | List the repositories and folders where work can happen, and mark the ones this task uses. It finds one by name, path or alias |

**Notes, links and files**

| Tool | What it does |
|---|---|
| `task_note_write` | Create a note, or edit one: replace the whole note, replace the section under one heading, or add to the end. A replace includes the version the agent last read, so if the note changed since then, Kepler refuses the replace rather than overwriting the note |
| `task_note_delete` | Delete a note. The task's **Prompt** cannot be deleted |
| `task_comment_reply` | Reply on a review comment you sent, so the answer shows on the comment's card in Kepler, and resolve the comment once the request is done. You can reopen it |
| `task_link_update` | Attach or detach issue, pull request and other links, which Kepler classifies, fetching each one's title and status when it can. An agent that starts a server for you to open (a dev server, Storybook, a preview) attaches its local URL to the task, and detaches it when it stops the server for good |
| `task_file_attach` | Attach files by path, linked rather than copied. The agent can instead attach a file it wrote in a temporary folder as a copy saved with the task, up to 10 MiB |
| `task_file_detach` | Detach files. A linked file stays on disk, and an uploaded copy is deleted |

**Worktrees**

| Tool | What it does |
|---|---|
| `worktree_create` | Create a worktree on a new branch and bind it to the task. The branch starts from the repository's remote default branch or from a base the agent names |
| `worktree_attach` | Bind a worktree or folder that already exists on disk to the task, without changing any files |
| `worktree_detach` | Remove a binding without touching the worktree, the branch, the files, or the sessions running there. The agent cannot detach the task's own folder or the place it runs in |
| `worktree_update` | Record a new merge target after the agent rebased a stacked branch or moved it onto another branch. A merge target you saved yourself takes precedence |
| `worktree_delete` | Delete a worktree from disk. Its branch goes too when Kepler finds it merged; an unmerged branch is kept unless the agent asks to delete it |

Where AI Sync and AI Compose are turned on, the `sync_*` and `compose_*` tools also let an agent update a branch from its base with a rebase or merge, and reorganize its commits. See [Review Changes](/kepler/review-changes#agent-tools-ai-sync-and-ai-compose).

**Progress and lifecycle**

| Tool | What it does |
|---|---|
| `task_create` | Create a *separate* task beside this one, with its own prompt, places, notes, links and files, for work that needs its own tracking. Kepler links it back to this task (as a sub-task, parent, follow-up, or related task), nothing starts on it, and it can go into a group, which is created if the name is new |
| `task_update` | Set the stage your board shows (**Exploration**, **In Development**, **In Review**, **Done**), put the task on hold or lift the hold, rename it, move it into or out of a group (a new name creates the group), restore it from the archive, or let Kepler set the stage again from Git and pull requests. If it replaces a stage or a hold you set, it tells you |
| `task_archive` | Archive a task. Archiving alone stops nothing and deletes nothing, and with cleanup, it also deletes the task's worktrees and their merged branches |

**Starting and coordinating work**

| Tool | What it does |
|---|---|
| `session_start` | Start an agent session on a task, as the starting session's child (a delegate, a reviewer, or a handoff), and send it a first message, in a place the agent names or in a new worktree. It uses the same agent, account, model, mode and effort unless the agent picks others from `agent_list`, and it can start without the task's context, as a reviewer would |
| `session_send` | Send another session a prompt to act on, or a message for its inbox. A session reports back to the session that started it with a status (progress, done, blocked or failed), and can also stop the other session's running turn |
| `session_update` | Rename a session. Sessions that run in the terminal or outside Kepler cannot be renamed |
| `session_archive` | Archive a session: its history stays and its agent stops. A session cannot archive itself |
| `inbox_read` | Read this session's inbox, or wait up to 60 seconds for reports from the sessions it started |
| `approval_list` | List every request waiting on your approval. It cannot approve or deny anything |
| `theme_get` / `theme_save` | Read Kepler's theme format, then check a theme file and install it into the themes folder |

### What runs at once, and what asks you

Every workspace tool is pre-approved, in Chat and in Terminal, so none of them shows the agent's own permission prompt. Instead, Kepler decides which requests can run at once.

An agent works freely within its own work. Its own work is its own task, plus the tasks and sessions it created or started sessions on. These requests run at once:

- Reads, anywhere.
- Creating a task, a note or a worktree.
- Changes inside the agent's own work, except changes that can lose something.

These requests wait for your approval:

- Sending a prompt to any session other than one the agent started itself, or a message to a session outside its own work
- Stopping or renaming a session outside its own work, or archiving any session other than one it started
- Changing a task outside its own work: its stage, hold, name, group, links or notes, or detaching its files. A group change reads on the card as *Put it in the group "{name}"*, *Create the group "{name}" and put it there*, or *Take it out of its group*
- Changing a Kepler setting that affects your accounts, privacy, other tools, what runs, or where files go. Only [Ask Kepler](/kepler/ask-kepler) can change settings, never a task's agent. The card names the setting and its change, *From {from} to {to}*, and offers no wider approval, so you approve each change on its own. See [Approval requests](/kepler/agent-sessions#approval-requests)
- Deleting any note
- Detaching an uploaded file, because Kepler deletes its saved copy
- Archiving a task outside its own work or with other live sessions, and any archive that also deletes worktrees
- Deleting a worktree that has something to lose (uncommitted changes, unpushed commits on a branch being deleted, commits on a detached HEAD, a status Kepler cannot read), or that another task is bound to
- Starting a session in a more permissive mode than the agent's own, or on a task outside its own work
- Overwriting a theme file when there is no Trash to keep the old one
- The AI Sync and Compose tools that change a repository or rewrite its history

Kepler compares modes on 3 levels, plan, edit and auto, and maps them onto each agent's own permission modes. A session that an agent starts cannot run in a higher mode than the session that started it unless you approve. The request says *More permissive than the asking session, which is in {mode} mode.*

The request appears as an approval card above the asking session's composer, with **Approve** and **Deny**. The **Approve** menu can approve every request of that kind from the session, or always. A rule you make with **Always approve** is listed under **Settings → Agents → Approvals**, where **Remove** deletes it. **Always approve** is not offered for actions that can lose work. See [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions#when-the-agent-asks-you-something).

The agent does not wait for you to answer the card. Kepler tells the agent the request is awaiting your approval, the agent continues, and the outcome arrives in its inbox. Before an approved request runs, Kepler checks again. If the target changed in the meantime, such as a worktree that has new commits, nothing runs.

`worktree_delete` has the same protection as your own delete. It refuses while a live session is running in the worktree, including the agent's own session. A worktree it deletes stays on the task, marked as gone, until someone detaches it.

### Reports between sessions

Each session has an **inbox** for what other agents send it:

- Reports and messages
- Changes in the state of a session it started
- The outcomes of its approval requests

When an item arrives for an idle session, Kepler wakes the session to read it. A busy session reads it when its turn ends. Kepler wakes sessions running in Terminal the same way. A session whose agent cannot reach Kepler's workspace tools does not receive state changes.

A session with unread reports has a badge with their count on its tab and on its row in the context panel. To have the agent read them now, click **Have it read them** above its composer.

Agents that keep waking each other can loop. To stop a loop, after 20 turns started by agents rather than by you, reports stop waking the session. The session reads *Reports from other agents are paused*. To turn wakes back on, click **Resume reports**, or send the session a message of your own.

---

---
# The Task View
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/task-view/
product: Kepler
feature: Tasks
content_type: how-to
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-10

Each task has its own screen, the **task page**. The context panel lists everything attached to the task. Beside it, the content area shows the sessions, working copies, files, and details you open.

To open the task page, double-click a task's row in [the Kepler interface](/kepler/kepler-interface), or click **Open task page** in the task's side panel. For what a task is and what you can attach to one, see [Tasks and Resources](/kepler/tasks-and-resources).

***

## The header

The header holds these controls, from left to right:

- **Hide context panel** or **Show context panel**, which hides and shows the context panel. See [The context panel](#the-context-panel).
- **Back to dashboard**, a back chevron, which returns you to the list exactly as you left it: the same segment, grouping, filters, and selection.
- **The task switcher**, the task's name as a chip, which jumps to another task without going back first. It searches as you type, and each row shows the same session status dots as the task list. Right-click the name for the same actions as the **⋮** menu, or double-click it to rename the task.
- **⋮ Task actions**, a menu of actions on the whole task. See [Task actions](#task-actions).
- **The Progress control**, which shows where the work stands: **Exploration**, **In Development**, **In Review**, **On hold**, or **Done**. Click it to set the stage yourself or to set it back to **Automatic**. An archived task shows **Archived** here instead. See [Arranging your work](/kepler/arranging-your-work).
- **Terminal**, at the right edge, which shows and hides the [terminal drawer](#the-terminal-drawer) and counts the terminals running in it.

When a task looks finished, the header shows a **Ready to archive?** prompt with **Archive** beside it. The prompt stays until you archive the task or dismiss the prompt.

### Task actions

The **⋮ Task actions** menu holds these items:

- The task's **Progress** submenu, with **Reopen** leading on a finished task.
- **Mark as read** while any of the task's sessions is unread, which marks them all read. Otherwise the menu offers **Mark as unread**.
- **Rename task**.
- **Copy task link**, which copies a Kepler link that opens this task.
- **Copy task prompt** and **Add resource…**.
- **Refresh**, which reads the task's worktrees and its pull requests and issues again. Right after a refresh, **Refresh** is unavailable for a short time, and its tooltip says when you can try again.
- **Shut down all agents**, while any are running.
- **Archive task** and **Delete task**. On an already-archived task, **Restore task** replaces **Archive task**.

### Rename a task

To rename a task, do one of the following:

- Pick **Rename task** in the **⋮ Task actions** menu.
- Press **F2** anywhere on the page outside a text field.
- Double-click the task switcher.

The name turns into an editable field. **Auto-name** (*Suggest a name from the task's prompt and resources*) fills the field with a suggestion that you can accept or edit. It never renames the task on its own. To save, press **Enter** or click the check mark. To cancel, press **Escape** or click **×**.

### On a phone

At phone width, for example in a phone browser connected through [Remote Access](/kepler/remote-environments#remote-access-reach-kepler-from-another-device), the task page replaces its header with a single bar:

- **Back**, on the left, which shows a dot when another task needs you.
- The task's name as a chip, which opens the task switcher. Swipe sideways on the name to go back to the previous task.
- A segment for each of **Sessions**, **Changes**, **Terminal**, and **Resources**. When the name would be cut off, **Resources** is the first segment to go.

Tap a segment to go to what needs you first, such as a blocked question, or else to the last session you had open. Each segment has a picker that lists that group's rows. From the picker, you can archive or close each row, or add another with **New session**, **New terminal**, or **Add resource**. On a phone, a terminal fills the whole column instead of a drawer.

Below the bar, a details row holds the Progress control, **Refresh**, and a fold chevron. Unfolded, it shows the checkout and its pull request and issue chips. It folds away while **Terminal** or **Changes** is on screen.

Pull down on the bar, or long-press a segment, to open **Everything in this task**. This sheet lists every session, checkout, terminal, and resource under the same group headings as the context panel, each with its own actions menu.
