- **A remote Electron window** reuses its model across reconnects and restarts, as long as you're returning to the same saved remote connection from the same desktop app. A different machine, a different profile, or a connection that falls back to a different port needs its own download. Until a Qwen3-ASR model is verified in that window, dictation there uses an installed Whisper model rather than failing or starting a download on its own.
- **Browser-based Remote Access** caches the model per browser, device, and profile. A different browser, device, or a private window needs its own download. The same browser returning to the same address can reuse what it already has, unless that browser has since cleared its storage.

Learned words and the languages this device has dictated in stay in the same storage, on the device in front of you, and never go to the remote machine.

See [Remote Environments](/kepler/remote-environments).

---

---
# Agent Integrations
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/agent-integrations/
product: Kepler
feature: Agent Integrations
content_type: how-to
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-10

Use **Settings → Agents** to install the coding agents you already use, sign in to them, and choose how they run in Kepler. You sign in with your own agent account, and Kepler adds no markup on the agents you bring.

Kepler supports 9 agents. You can also add any other agent that speaks the Agent Client Protocol (ACP), or whose command-line interface you want to run inside a task.

***

## Supported agents

Each agent gets its own section in **Settings → Agents**, in this order:

| Agent | Name in Settings | How Kepler runs it | Run modes | Multiple accounts |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Claude Code** | Claude Code | Your installed `claude` CLI | Chat or Terminal | Yes |
| **Codex** | Codex | Your installed `codex` CLI | Chat or Terminal | Yes |
| **GitHub Copilot** | GitHub Copilot | Your installed `copilot` CLI in ACP mode (`--acp`) | Chat or Terminal | Yes |
| **OpenCode** | OpenCode | Your installed `opencode` CLI, v2, in ACP mode (`acp`) | Chat or Terminal | No |
| **Pi** | Pi | Your installed `pi` CLI, in its own terminal interface | Terminal only | No |
| **Auggie** | Auggie | Your installed `auggie` CLI in ACP mode (`--acp`) | Chat or Terminal | Yes |
| **Google Antigravity** | Antigravity | Your installed `agy` CLI in a terminal, or Google's separate Antigravity ACP server (`agy_acp_server`) for Chat | Terminal (default) or Chat | No |
| **Cursor** | Cursor | Your installed `cursor-agent` CLI in ACP mode (`acp`) | Chat or Terminal | No |
| **Grok Build** | Grok Build | Your installed `grok` CLI in ACP mode (`agent stdio`) | Chat or Terminal | Yes |

**Auggie** is Augment's coding agent. It runs over ACP like the other agents, and its model and mode pickers work like any other agent's. Auggie is also one of the 3 agents that report plan usage back to Kepler, with Claude Code and Codex. Auggie reports only its credit balance, with the credits your plan includes, rather than usage windows. To learn about the plan usage meter, see [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions#usage-indicators).

Kepler asks each agent's provider for plan usage while **Check plan usage with each agent's provider** is on. This setting is in **Settings → Agents → Usage limits**, and it is on by default.

**Grok Build** is xAI's coding agent. It signs in through your browser, or you can supply an xAI API key. Grok Build keeps its data under `~/.grok`, and Kepler uses that folder to keep several accounts apart.

**Google Antigravity runs 2 separate binaries.** Terminal mode runs the `agy` CLI. Chat mode runs Google's Antigravity ACP server, which is a separate download with its own version. The agent's section in **Settings → Agents** lists both under **Components**: **Antigravity CLI** (*Needed for Terminal mode.*) and **ACP server** (*Rich-text (ACP) mode. Installed separately from the Antigravity CLI.*). Each has its own **Install** or **Update to {version}**. Either one alone is enough to use the agent in that mode. Sessions stay in Terminal until you pick **Chat** for Antigravity, because the ACP server signs in separately from the CLI.

**Pi is terminal-only.** Its CLI has no ACP mode, so Kepler runs Pi's own interface in a terminal inside the task instead of leaving Pi out. Kepler does not check Pi's sign-in. Pi uses its own sign-in (`/login`, or the provider API-key environment variables it reads directly).

With Pi 1.x, Kepler loads its own extension for each launch. The extension gives the session the task's context and Kepler's workspace tools, and leaves your `APPEND_SYSTEM.md` and `~/.pi/agent` untouched. With other Pi versions, Kepler pastes the task's context in instead. A Pi session resumes by its own session ID, and Pi does not ask again whether to trust a worktree of a repository you already trust.

**OpenCode needs version 2.** Kepler reads and resumes only OpenCode 2's sessions and will not start a session on an OpenCode 1 binary: its card warns *OpenCode {version} is not supported*. A conversation you started under OpenCode 1 resumes from OpenCode 2's copy of it.

**Inbox wake in Terminal mode.** Kepler can wake an idle **Terminal** session to read its inbox for Claude Code, Pi, and OpenCode 2.1.1 or newer. Pi gets the wake through Kepler's per-launch extension and OpenCode through a plugin Kepler loads for each launch, and neither touches your own config. Kepler delivers the wake as a queued follow-up prompt. Other agents in Terminal mode cannot use Kepler's workspace tools or inbox, and Kepler suggests **Continue in Chat** from the session menu instead.

**Claude Code folder trust.** Kepler reads folder trust where the Claude Code CLI records your answer. A worktree inherits the trust you already gave its repository, so a session does not stop at the trust prompt.

**Codex now runs your own CLI.** Earlier builds shipped a bundled `codex-acp` engine. Kepler now finds and starts the `codex` you have installed, like every other agent, so its section reads **Installed** and it has a binary picker.

You set the mode the same way for every agent that offers both. **Settings → Agents → *your agent* → New sessions start in** picks between **Chat** and **Terminal**, per agent. To start one session the other way, use **Start in** in the composer's **Agent settings**. See [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions#how-a-session-runs).

These 2 agents need a recent build to run over ACP:

| Agent | Minimum |
|---|---|
| **GitHub Copilot** | CLI v1.0 or newer. Older builds reject `--acp` |
| **Cursor CLI** | A build that exposes the `acp` command, added in early 2026 |

Kepler checks both before it starts a session and tells you to update rather than failing with a protocol error.

***

## Install an agent

When an agent is not installed, its section reads **Not installed** and offers **Install**. Kepler runs the install command for you and shows the output as it runs, so you can read a failure rather than guess at one. **Cancel** stops an install in progress (*Install cancelled: {name}*). Installs and updates run one at a time. If you start a second one while one is running, it waits. An install or update that produces no result for 20 minutes stops on its own and says so in the output.

The install methods depend on the operating system of the machine you are on:

| Agent | macOS | Linux | Windows |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Claude Code** | Native installer, Homebrew, npm (global) | Native installer, npm (global) | Native installer, winget, npm (global) |
| **Codex** | Standalone installer, Homebrew, npm (global) | Standalone installer, npm (global) | npm (global) |
| **GitHub Copilot** | Native installer, Homebrew, npm (global) | Native installer, Homebrew, npm (global) | winget, npm (global) |
| **Cursor CLI** | Native installer, Homebrew | Native installer | Native installer |
| **Auggie** | npm (global) | npm (global) | npm (global) |
| **OpenCode** | Native installer, Homebrew, npm (global) | Native installer, Homebrew, npm (global), pacman | npm (global) |
| **Grok Build** | Native installer | Native installer | Native installer |
| **Pi** | npm (global) | npm (global) | npm (global) |
| **Google Antigravity** | Native installer, plus the ACP server component | Native installer, plus the ACP server component | Native installer, plus the ACP server component |

Every OpenCode method installs OpenCode 2. Windows offers only npm, because Scoop's and Chocolatey's `opencode` packages still install OpenCode 1.

If an agent offers no install method for your OS, Kepler says so and points you to the custom binary path instead.

Kepler does not close the install output pane automatically when the install finishes. Errors during the install, such as a permissions failure, a partial install, or a post-install warning, appear only in that pane, so read them before you dismiss it.

***

## Binary detection

Kepler resolves each agent's binary the way your shell does: the first match on your `PATH`, so it agrees with `which`. Beyond `PATH`, it also searches your login shell's environment and well-known install directories. This is how Kepler finds an agent installed by nvm or Homebrew, even when you did not launch Kepler from a terminal. Kepler reads your login shell again on **Restart agent**, **Re-scan**, or a retry, so an environment variable you add, change, or remove in your shell's startup files reaches the restarted agent without restarting Kepler.

Each agent's card in **Settings → Agents** shows what Kepler resolved. The version and **Install** are in the card's title line. **Binary**, **Components**, and **Data folder** are under **Program and data folder**:

| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| Version | The installed version, or **Not installed** |
| **Install** | Runs one of the install methods above. Shown when the agent is not installed |
| **Binary** | The resolved absolute path, or **Not found**, with where it came from (**PATH**, **Shell**, or **Common**) and its version |
| **Re-scan** | Re-detects this agent's binary. Use it after installing or removing one outside Kepler |
| **Custom path…** | Pins an absolute path of your own. Kepler validates it and refuses a directory or a path that is not a file |
| **Clear custom** | Drops the pinned path and goes back to automatic resolution. Shown only while a custom path is set |
| **Installed versions** | A picker listing every install Kepler found, with an **Auto** row. Appears only when Kepler finds more than one |
| **Data folder** | Overrides the agent's own data and config directory. Leave it empty for the agent default |
| **Enabled** | Whether Kepler offers this agent when you start a session |

If Kepler cannot read an installed agent's version, its section shows a **Version unknown** badge rather than plain **Installed**: *Kepler was unable to read {name}'s version. Features that depend on the version stay off, such as sending a new session's first message automatically. Reinstalling or updating {name} usually fixes this.*

When an installed version has a known problem, the agent's card shows a warning note under its title line that names the version and what to do:

| Agent | Warning |
|---|---|
| **OpenCode** | *OpenCode {version} is not supported*. Sessions with it do not start, so install OpenCode 2 or pick an OpenCode 2 binary |
| **Auggie** | *Auggie {version} may not load your MCP servers in chat* |
| **Google Antigravity** | *ACP server {version} can fail to start on Linux*. Reinstall the ACP server under **Program and data folder** |
| **Codex** | *Codex {version} can show approval prompts that need no answer*. Update Codex to 0.163.0 or newer |

If a pinned path later disappears (for example, when an auto-updater cleans up an old version), Kepler falls back to automatic resolution instead of reporting the agent as missing.

Above the agent cards in **Settings → Agents**, **Re-scan** re-detects every agent at once, and **Update all** runs each installed agent's own updater.

***

## Sign in to an agent

An installed agent shows **Sign in** until it has a credential, and **Sign out** once it does. **Sign in** opens a modal listing the methods that agent supports on this machine, plus any methods Kepler provides itself:

| Agent | How you sign in |
|---|---|
| **Claude Code** | Browser sign-in. Kepler runs the sign-in for you and your browser opens; you paste a code back only if the browser callback cannot reach Kepler. **More sign-in options** adds **Amazon Bedrock**, **Google Vertex AI**, **Microsoft Foundry**, and **LLM gateway** |
| **Codex** | Sign in with a ChatGPT account through your browser, or enter an API key. On a remote, **ChatGPT (device code)** |
| **GitHub Copilot** | **Sign in with GitHub**: Kepler's own device flow. Open `github.com/login/device` and enter the one-time code |
| **Cursor CLI** | Cursor's own browser sign-in, driven from the modal, or **Paste an API key** from the Cursor dashboard. On a remote, only the API key works |
| **Auggie** | **Sign in with browser**, or **Paste session token** |
| **OpenCode** | **OpenCode account (Go or Console)**: sign in through your browser with a one-time code. OpenCode also resolves providers from its own config file and provider environment variables |
| **Grok Build** | Browser sign-in, or **Paste an API key** for a deployment with no local browser |
| **Google Antigravity** | **Google OAuth**, **Google Cloud project**, or **Google Cloud project (SSO)**, driven from the modal. The ACP server used for Chat keeps its own sign-in, so Kepler checks whichever one the mode you picked uses |
| **Pi** | Nothing to do in Kepler. Sign in inside the CLI itself, or set the provider environment variables it reads |

### Claude Code through a cloud provider or gateway

To run Claude Code through your cloud provider rather than a Claude account, click **More sign-in options** in the **Sign in to Claude Code** modal and pick a method:

| Method | What you enter |
|---|---|
| **Amazon Bedrock** | A Bedrock API key (`AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK`) and the AWS region (`AWS_REGION`) |
| **Google Vertex AI** | The project (`ANTHROPIC_VERTEX_PROJECT_ID`) and region (`CLOUD_ML_REGION`), and optionally a credentials file (`GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS`). Leave the file empty to use application default credentials |
| **Microsoft Foundry** | The resource name only (`ANTHROPIC_FOUNDRY_RESOURCE`), and optionally an API key and your Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku deployment names. Without a key, it signs in with Microsoft Entra ID credentials on this machine |
| **LLM gateway** | The gateway's URL (`ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`) and the token it issues (`ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN`), plus any other `NAME=value` variables your gateway needs |

The account then reads as the provider and its region, project, or resource, or as the gateway's host. Kepler shows no plan usage for it, because the plan belongs to your cloud provider. Saving one method clears the values stored for the others, and **Sign out** clears the provider. You can set a gateway's extra variables only on the computer running Kepler, not from a paired device.

### OpenCode account

**OpenCode account (Go or Console)** signs OpenCode in to your OpenCode account:

1. Click **Sign in** on OpenCode's card and pick **OpenCode account (Go or Console)**.
2. Click **Open sign-in in browser** and enter the **One-time code** the modal shows.
3. Choose the workspace with your Go subscription.
4. Select a Go model to use your plan.

The agent's card then shows OpenCode as signed in.

### Browser sign-in, including on a remote

**Claude Code** and **Codex** both sign in through your browser, and neither needs a terminal to do it.

This also works on a [remote environment](/kepler/remote-environments):

- **Claude Code** on a remote offers **Sign in with browser**, which opens the sign-in page in your *local* browser and takes the code you paste back. Kepler saves the credential on the remote machine.
- **Codex** on a remote offers **ChatGPT (device code)**: *Sign in with a one-time code in your browser. Works on any remote.* Kepler shows the sign-in link and a **One-time code**. The remote CLI waits for you to finish and writes the token there. Some ChatGPT workspaces turn device sign-in off, and Kepler then points you to the alternatives.
- **Cursor CLI** on a remote offers only **Paste an API key**, because its browser sign-in cannot complete there.

Wherever Kepler opens a browser sign-in for Claude Code, Codex, or Antigravity, **Open sign-in in browser** appears beside a read-only **Sign-in link** field with **Copy link**. To open the link in another browser or profile, copy it. The field stays after the browser opens, because a browser can open somewhere you cannot see it. The field goes away if the sign-in attempt fails.

When a sign-in runs in a terminal on a remote and the browser page does not load after you sign in, paste that page's address into the box under the terminal (*Browser page won't load after you sign in? Paste its address here.*) and click **Send**. Kepler requests the address on the remote machine, and only when the sign-in itself printed it. You then finish in the terminal.

**Import local Codex login** is the other remote route, in the desktop app: it copies this machine's `~/.codex/auth.json` to the remote target, and asks you to confirm on this machine before it reads the file. The import copies a credential: anyone with access to that remote machine can send Codex requests on your account until you sign out.

A Codex API key works locally and on a remote: Kepler collects the key in the modal and passes it to Codex for that account. **Sign out** on Codex signs the CLI itself out, and Kepler follows a sign-in you do in the Codex CLI outside Kepler.

### Auggie's sign-in methods

Auggie supports 2 sign-in methods:

| Method | What it does | Where it works |
|---|---|---|
| **Sign in with browser** | Runs Auggie's sign-in and finishes it in your browser. Auggie stores the credential under `~/.augment` | Local, and over SSH: the remote variant opens the page in your local browser and takes a pasted JSON response |
| **Paste session token** | You paste the JSON from `auggie token print` into Kepler. Kepler stores it and supplies it on every session | Anywhere, including CI-style setups with no browser |

If you run Auggie's browser sign-in on this machine yourself, Kepler detects it and you can skip the token paste.

### Multiple accounts of one agent

**Claude Code**, **Codex**, **GitHub Copilot**, **Auggie**, and **Grok Build** support more than one signed-in account. To add one, open **Settings → Agents → *your agent* → Accounts** and click **Add account**. Each account keeps its own credentials and history.

To give each added account its own color, pick one from the swatch at the left of its row: **Rose**, **Amber**, **Lime**, **Cyan**, **Blue**, or **Violet**. Kepler tints the agent icon with that color on session tabs, the task's context panel, and the terminal status bar, so you can tell sessions on different accounts apart. *The default account stays uncolored.* Accounts also appear on the agent's card in Settings.

For **Auggie**, you can only add a second account with **Paste session token**. Its browser sign-in writes to one fixed file, so it would sign the second account into the first account's identity.

***

## Run modes

Most agents run in 2 modes, and each agent keeps its own default. To pick the default for an agent, open **Settings → Agents**, expand the agent, and set **New sessions start in**:

| Mode | What you get |
|---|---|
| **Chat** | *{agent} built into Kepler, with replies, diffs and plans you can read, review and search.* Kepler drives the agent over ACP and renders the conversation itself. This is the default |
| **Terminal** | *{agent}'s own command-line app, with its commands, shortcuts and settings, just as you use it today.* It runs in an embedded terminal inside the task |

To start one session in the other mode without changing the default, set **Start in** in the composer's **Agent settings** before you send the first message. An agent that offers only one mode shows no switch at all. See [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions#how-a-session-runs).

### Detecting sessions started outside Kepler

**Settings → Integrations → Your terminal → Show sessions started outside Kepler** is a separate setting that applies to all agents, and it is **on by default**. It installs GitKraken hooks so sessions you start in your own terminal show up in Kepler. It covers every agent Kepler can track that way: **Claude Code**, **Codex**, **Cursor**, **GitHub Copilot**, **OpenCode**, **Auggie**, **Grok Build**, and **Pi**. Kepler does not track Google Antigravity this way. See [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions#sessions-started-outside-kepler).

Kepler also follows its own **Terminal** sessions through those hooks. If a live terminal session keeps reporting status but its hook events stop arriving, Kepler warns *Agent sessions aren't reporting to Kepler*, because status and notifications may be out of date. **Repair** reinstalls the reporting configuration. Restart any session that still does not report afterward. A window that only views another computer's sessions gets the warning without **Repair**, because you repair reporting on the computer running the sessions.

### Programs that report their own status

Some terminal programs report their own status to Kepler (through the OSC 7501 escape sequence). When an agent's terminal program does this, Kepler shows the session as working, blocked, or done from what the program reports, without hooks. If hook events also arrive, the hooks take precedence. See [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions#whats-different-in-terminal).

***

## Your default agent

**Settings → Tasks → New tasks → Default agent** sets which agent is preselected when you start work, and supplies the model, mode, and thinking effort a new session starts with.

Kepler saves agent options **per account**. Picking a different account of the same agent brings up that account's own saved model and options, so a larger model you chose on your work account does not carry over to your personal one.

Only agents that are installed and **Enabled** appear in the picker. If your saved default is no longer installed, Kepler says so and asks you to pick another.

An Action can override all of this. See [Actions](/kepler/actions) for how an Action pins a provider, account, model, mode, and options together, and which choice wins when they disagree.

***

## Custom agents

If your agent is not one of the 9 supported agents, you can add it by its command. To add one, open **Settings → Agents → Custom agents**, click **New custom agent**, and fill in these fields:

| Field | What it holds |
|---|---|
| **Name** | What the agent is called in Kepler's pickers |
| **Runs in** | **Chat**: *Kepler's chat. Needs a program that speaks ACP (the Agent Client Protocol).* **Terminal**: *The command's own app, in a terminal.* |
| **Command** | The binary to run: an absolute path, or a name Kepler resolves on your `PATH` |
| **Args (one per line)** | Arguments for the command. For a Chat agent, the arguments that put it into ACP mode, for example `--acp` |
| **Environment variables (KEY=value, one per line)** | Variables merged into the agent's environment on every session |

Kepler treats environment values as secrets: it encrypts them at rest, hides them after you save, and never sends them to any client. When you edit a custom agent, leaving a value empty (`KEY=`) keeps the stored secret, and typing a new value replaces it.

Custom agents appear alongside the built-in agents everywhere you can choose an agent. A custom agent that runs in **Terminal** works the same way: Kepler works out what terminal mode can offer from the command's own flags rather than from a list of agent names, so your own agent degrades exactly the way a built-in one does.

***

## MCP servers

Kepler lists the MCP servers each agent loads, and lets you add, remove, sign in to, and turn off servers or single tools, per repository from the composer's **Agent settings** pill or as defaults in **Settings → Agents → MCP servers**. See [MCP Servers](/kepler/mcp-servers).

***

## What Kepler tells the agent about itself

Agent CLIs report **Kepler** as the client name, so your sessions show up as Kepler in places like your Anthropic dashboard rather than as an unlabeled non-interactive run.

This labeling applies to the sessions Kepler drives over ACP. **Terminal** mode deliberately leaves the label alone, because overriding it there would break key handling in the embedded terminal.

***

## Sessions

After you connect an agent, you run it in a **session** inside a task. To learn how to start and resume sessions, queue prompts, and review what the agent produced, see [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions).

A task holds resources and does not require a worktree, or even a repository. See [Tasks and Resources](/kepler/tasks-and-resources).

To follow conversations you started outside Kepler, see [Sessions started outside Kepler](/kepler/agent-sessions#sessions-started-outside-kepler).

---

---
# MCP Servers
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/mcp-servers/
product: Kepler
feature: MCP Servers
content_type: how-to
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-10

Your coding agents load **Model Context Protocol** (**MCP**) servers from their own config files. Kepler reads those files and lists exactly the servers each agent loads. From Kepler, without editing the agent's config by hand, you can:

- See the servers each agent loads.
- Turn a server, or one of its tools, off where you do not want it.
- Add or remove a server.
- Sign in to a server that needs it.

You manage MCP servers in 3 places:

- Per repository, from the composer's **Agent settings** pill
- Per repository, in **Settings → Repositories →** *repository* **→ MCP servers**
- As global defaults, in **Settings → Agents → MCP servers**

**Requirements and limits**

- Works for **Claude Code**, **Codex**, **GitHub Copilot**, **Cursor**, **OpenCode**, **Auggie**, and **Grok Build**. Pi, Antigravity, and custom agents do not expose their MCP servers to Kepler. For these agents, the manager reads *This agent does not expose its MCP servers to Kepler.*
- The agent must be installed. Settings lists only the agents that answer.
- Kepler shows the servers the agent's config files define. Kepler does not list servers that are not stored on disk, such as claude.ai connectors.

***

## Where you manage them

| Where | What a change applies to |
|---|---|
| The composer's **Agent settings** pill → **MCP servers** → **Manage** | This repository, for that agent |
| **Settings → Repositories →** *repository* **→ MCP servers** | This repository, for the agent you pick |
| **Settings → Agents → MCP servers** | Every repository, as the default each one inherits |

The **MCP servers** dialog in the composer includes **Open repo settings**, which opens the same list in **Settings → Repositories**.

Every place shows the same manager. It groups servers by where they are defined:

| Group | Where the server comes from |
|---|---|
| **Added by you** | Your own config for the agent, used in every repository |
| **In this repo, shared with your team** | Checked into this repository |
| **In this repo, just you** | This repository only, not shared |
| **From plugins** | Installed by a plugin |
| **Set by your organization** | Managed by your organization |

Each row is a server. The switch on a row turns the server on or off, and clicking the row opens the server's own page. A row can carry these badges:

- **Sign in needed**: the server needs authentication before the agent can use it.
- **Every repo**: a change to the server reaches every repository.
- **Locked**: *Kepler cannot edit this entry in the agent's config file*, such as a server your organization manages.

***

## Per repository

To manage the servers for one repository:

1. In a session or in the **New task** composer, open the **Agent settings** pill. Its **MCP servers** row reads *{enabled} of {total} enabled*.
2. Click **Manage**. The **MCP servers** dialog opens. Its subtitle reads *{agent} in {repo}*, the agent and the repository the dialog applies to.

When you open a server's page, **All servers** takes you back to the list.

A change here applies to that repository only. Worktrees of one checkout share the setting, so a server you turn off in a repository stays off in every task's worktree of it.

If a server is off in Settings and you have not turned it on here, the server says *Off for every repo in Settings. Turn it on to use it here.*, with **Open Settings** to go to the global default. Turning it on in the dialog turns it on for this repository only.

### Turn off a single tool

A server's page lists its **Tools** under the **Let {agent} use this server** switch. Kepler connects to the server to ask for its tools, so the list can take a moment to load (*Asking the server for its tools…*). If the server needs authentication first, the list reads *Sign in to this server to see its tools.*

To turn off one tool, open the server's page and turn off the tool's switch. *Turn a tool off to keep {agent} from calling it.*

Turning off a single tool works for Claude Code, Codex, and Grok Build. For the other agents, turn the whole server off instead.

***

## Global defaults

**Settings → Agents → MCP servers** is the same manager with no repository. Its description reads *Give your agents extra tools, like a database, a browser or your issue tracker.* Use the **Agent** picker at the top to choose the agent, and the account when that agent has more than one.

**Keep the GitKraken MCP server installed in every agent** is on by default. *Gives every command-line agent Git tools and your issues and pull requests through GitKraken. Turn off to manage it yourself.*

The repository and global levels combine like this:

- A repository uses the global value until you change that server in its own dialog.
- A repository's choice wins over the global one, in either direction: a repository can turn off a server that's on globally, or turn on a server that's off globally.
- Kepler stores a choice only while it differs from the level beneath it, so switching a server back to match the global default hands control back to the default.

You cannot change plugin servers or Cursor servers in Settings, although plugin servers are listed there. Cursor keeps its on and off state per project, so switch a Cursor server from a repository's dialog instead.

***

## Add and remove servers

To add a server, click **Add server**: beside the section's heading in Settings, or at the foot of the list in the MCP servers dialog. The **Add MCP server ({agent})** page opens with these fields:

| Field | What it takes |
|---|---|
| **Name** | Letters, numbers, `.`, `_`, or `-`, up to 64 characters, unique where it is saved |
| **Applies to** | **Every repo**, **This repo only**, or **This repo, shared with your team**. The choices depend on the agent and on whether you are in a repository, and the field shows only when there is more than 1 choice, as in a repository's **MCP servers** section |
| **Runs as** | **Command** for a local server, or **URL** or **URL (SSE)** for a remote one |
| **Command** and **Arguments** | For a command server, for example `npx -y @some/server` |
| **URL** | For a remote server, an `http://` or `https://` address |
| **Environment variables** / **Headers** | Key and value pairs. Values stay hidden until you choose **Show value** |

Kepler writes the new server into the agent's own config file, in the format that agent uses, so the agent's CLI sees it too.

To remove a server, open the server's page and click **Remove server**. Kepler deletes the server from the agent's config. You cannot undo this.

You cannot remove these servers from Kepler:

- Plugin servers.
- Managed servers.
- GitHub Copilot servers defined in a repository. You can remove only the Copilot servers in your own config.

***

## Copy a server to other agents

To use a server you already set up with another agent or account, copy it instead of adding it again. Kepler copies the server's full definition, including its environment variables and headers.

1. Open the server's page.
2. Click **Also add to…**.
3. Select each agent, or each account of an agent, that should get the server.
4. Click **Add to *N* destinations**.

Kepler adds the server to each destination in turn. If one copy fails, the others still go ahead, and the failed destination stays selected with its error.

You cannot copy servers from plugins, so their page does not show **Also add to…**.

***

## Sign in to a server

For a server that needs authentication, its page has a **Sign-in** section. It offers **Sign in**, or **Re-authenticate** once you are signed in, and **Clear authentication** to sign the server out. Kepler signs in by running the agent's own CLI, under the same account the session uses, so the credentials end up where the agent looks for them. Sign-in is available for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and Cursor servers.

In a local window, **Open sign-in page** opens your browser, and Kepler finishes when you are done (*Finish signing in in your browser*). In a window connected to a remote environment, sign in on that page, then paste the URL you land on into **Redirect URL**.

***

## When changes apply

| Where the change lands | When it takes effect |
|---|---|
| A Claude Code **Chat** session | Straight away. Kepler reconnects the session with the new servers and keeps the conversation and your model and mode picks |
| A terminal session, or any other agent's session | On restart. The **Agent settings** pill and the dialog show *{count} MCP changes apply when the agent restarts.* with **Restart agent** |
| The **New task** composer | The session you start comes up with that state |

Where Kepler saves an on or off choice depends on the agent:

- **Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, and GitHub Copilot**: Kepler does not edit the agent's config. Kepler keeps the choice itself and passes it to the agent when the agent launches, so the same agent run from your own terminal is not affected. The one exception is turning on a Claude Code server that Claude's own config lists as disabled: Kepler can do this only by editing that list.
- **Cursor and Grok Build**: Kepler writes the change into the agent's own files, which their CLIs also read.
- **Auggie**: Kepler lists the servers without a switch, because Auggie has no way to turn a server off. To stop using a server, edit Auggie's config.

Adding and removing a server always edits the config file.

Each agent account keeps its own MCP setup. When Kepler launches a Claude Code account other than the default one, it first copies in the default account's servers.

***

## Related

- [Agent Settings](/kepler/settings-agents#mcp-servers): **Settings → Agents**, including the **MCP servers** section.
- [Agent Integrations](/kepler/agent-integrations): the agents Kepler runs and how to set them up.
- [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions): the composer's **Agent settings** pill, and restarting a session.

---

---
# Issue Tracker Integrations
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/issue-tracker-integrations/
product: Kepler
feature: Issue Tracker Integrations
content_type: how-to
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-10

Connect an issue tracker to see the issues you are working on in [the Kepler interface](/kepler/kepler-interface), alongside your pull requests and the tasks you already have running. To start work on an issue, you pick its row instead of describing the work from scratch.

You manage providers in the **Issues and pull requests** section of **Settings → Integrations**.

***

## Trackers Kepler can read issues from

Of Kepler's 12 providers, 10 return issues:

| Provider | Also returns pull requests |
|---|---|
| **GitHub** | Yes |
| **GitHub Enterprise** | Yes |
| **GitLab** | Yes |
| **GitLab Self-Hosted** | Yes |
| **Azure DevOps** | Yes |
| **Azure DevOps Server** | Yes |
| **Jira** | No |
| **Jira Server / Data Center** | No |
| **Linear** | No |
| **Trello** | No |

The other 2 providers, **Bitbucket** and **Bitbucket Data Center**, return pull requests only. See [Pull Request Integrations](/kepler/pull-request-integrations).

Kepler supports self-hosted instances. **GitHub Enterprise**, **GitLab Self-Hosted**, **Azure DevOps Server**, and **Jira Server / Data Center** read issues the same way their cloud counterparts do, and 2 servers of the same kind stay separate even when their issue keys overlap. Which fields come back depends on your server's version, and your machine needs to be able to reach the server. You connect a self-hosted instance inside Kepler with its address and a personal access token. See [Connect a self-hosted tracker](#connect-a-self-hosted-tracker).

Kepler trusts the certificates installed in your operating system's certificate store, so a server signed by your company's own certificate authority, or a network that re-signs HTTPS traffic, works without extra setup.

***

## Connect a tracker

To connect a cloud tracker (**GitHub**, **GitLab**, **Azure DevOps**, **Jira**, **Linear**, or **Trello**), follow these steps:

1. Open **Settings → Integrations**.
2. Find the provider in **Issues and pull requests** and click **Connect**.
3. Authorize Kepler in the browser window that opens.
4. Return to Kepler, where the provider shows a **Connected** badge in **Issues and pull requests**.

Integrations belong to your GitKraken account, not to this copy of Kepler, so a provider you connect here is also available to the `gk` command-line interface (CLI) and GitKraken Desktop. To manage integrations, sign in to a GitKraken account. Kepler prompts you if you are not signed in.

For a cloud tracker, **Connect** sends you to GitKraken's website to authorize. Kepler opens `/connect` there in your system browser, names the provider, and includes a redirect back into Kepler. When you return, Kepler fetches your providers again instead of reusing its cached list.

While you authorize, Kepler keeps a **Connect {provider} in your browser** dialog open, with the provider's name in place of {provider}. If your browser did not open, copy the **Connection link** from the dialog and open it in a browser yourself. **Try again** makes a new link, because each link works once.

The dialog closes by itself as soon as the new connection appears, and Kepler checks for it again whenever you come back to a Kepler window. If Kepler cannot start the connection, the dialog reads **Unable to connect {provider}** and says why.

### Connect a self-hosted tracker

**GitHub Enterprise**, **GitLab Self-Hosted**, **Azure DevOps Server**, and **Jira Server / Data Center** connect inside Kepler with a personal access token rather than through the browser:

1. Open **Settings → Integrations**.
2. Find the provider in **Issues and pull requests** and click **Connect**. The **Connect {name}** dialog opens.
3. In **Server URL**, enter the server's address, including the port and installation path when your server uses them.
4. In **Personal access token**, paste a token with access to the issues you need.
5. Click **Save connection**.

Kepler checks the token against the server from your machine, keeps it in a protected credential store on this device, and syncs the connection to your GitKraken account. The dialog reports one of these results:

- The server accepted the token.
- Kepler saved the token without being able to reach the server or verify its certificate.
- The server refused the token: *The server refused this token. Check its value and permissions.*

For every message the dialog shows, see [Pull Request Integrations](/kepler/pull-request-integrations#connect-a-self-hosted-instance). Until Kepler finishes syncing the connection to your account, the provider's row shows **Cloud sync pending**. **Reconnect** on a self-hosted provider opens the same dialog, so you can replace an expired or rejected token there.

Use these controls to manage connected providers:

| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Reconnect** | Runs authorization again. Use it when a sign-in has expired |
| **Disconnect** | Removes the provider's primary connection. See [Disconnect a provider](#disconnect-a-provider) |
| **Refresh** | At the top of the section, checks every provider again |

A provider's row can also show a warning:

| Warning | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| **Sign-in expired** | The provider's sign-in has expired | Kepler tries to refresh the token on its own; **Reconnect** refreshes it by hand |
| **Cannot connect to server** | Kepler could not reach the provider's server. The integration is still connected | You do not need to reconnect. Check that the server is up and reachable from your network or VPN; the warning clears once the server answers |
| **Unexpected response** | The provider answered with data Kepler could not read, so some of its items may be missing. The integration is still connected | Reconnecting does not fix it. If the warning stays, check for a proxy or gateway between Kepler and the provider |
| An organization named under the row | One organization refuses Kepler's access, so its items are left out while everything else still loads. For example, Kepler names a GitHub organization that restricts OAuth app access, with a **Request access on GitHub** link | Follow the advice on the row, which names who can remove the restriction |

You do not have to open Settings to find a failing provider. Todo, the **Add resources** lists, and a link preview name it too, with the one fix that applies: **Reconnect**, **Reconnect in settings** for a self-hosted provider, **Open settings**, or **Retry**. See [Pull Request Integrations](/kepler/pull-request-integrations#where-your-pull-requests-turn-up) for each warning.

***

## Choose what Kepler brings in

Each connected integration has a visibility line under its row in **Settings → Integrations**. The line reads **Everything visible**, or **{count} hidden** with the number of items you have hidden. Trello has no visibility line.

To hide part of an integration:

1. Click **Choose what's visible…** on the provider's row. The **Choose what {name} brings in** dialog opens.
2. Clear the checkbox of each item to hide. Type in **Filter…** to narrow a long list.
3. Click **Save**.

What the dialog lists depends on the provider:

| Provider | Lists |
|---|---|
| **GitHub**, **GitHub Enterprise**, **GitLab**, **GitLab Self-Hosted**, **Bitbucket**, **Bitbucket Data Center** | **Organizations** and **Repositories** |
| **Azure DevOps**, **Azure DevOps Server** | **Organizations**, **Repositories**, and **Projects** |
| **Jira**, **Jira Server / Data Center**, **Linear** | **Projects** |

A ticked item is visible. Hiding an organization also hides its repositories, which show *Hidden with its organization* and cannot be ticked on their own. A hidden project leaves the issue lists but stays in the project pickers. A project that has not returned any issues yet may be missing from the dialog's list.

Hidden items are left out of Todo, the issue and pull request lists, and the pickers. Tasks and branches already linked to a hidden item keep resolving. Kepler stores the choice on your GitKraken account, so it follows you to other machines where you sign in.

***

## More than one account of the same provider

You can connect several accounts of the same provider: two GitHub accounts, a work Jira site and a personal one. When a provider has two or more, an **Accounts** list appears under its row with one entry per account.

Each entry carries two independent controls:

| Control | What it changes | How far it reaches |
|---|---|---|
| **Read from this account** | Which account Kepler reads this provider's issues and pull requests from | Kepler only, and non-destructive |
| **Set as primary** / **Primary** | The provider's primary account | Everywhere: other Kepler windows, the `gk` CLI, and GitKraken Desktop |

**Browsing a secondary account does not change your primary.** Selecting **Read from this account** on a second account switches what Kepler shows you and leaves the primary as it is. That is why **Read from this account** is a radio control instead of a button. The primary is the default read account, so a provider with no override reads through it.

Changing either one clears that provider's saved filters, because an organization or project from the old account might not exist on the new one. Kepler then fetches the list again.

**Reconnect keeps your choices.** When one account's sign-in fails, **Reconnect** renews that account's connection without disconnecting it first. When the same account connects again, its new connection takes the old one's place, as primary or as the read account if it was either, and Kepler removes the old one. Another account of the provider never becomes primary by accident.

The read account also authenticates Git. When you start work on an issue in a repository you have never cloned, Kepler clones that repository with the same connection it reads through. See [Pull Request Integrations](/kepler/pull-request-integrations) for which hosts this covers and what happens on the hosts it does not.

**Linear connections stay separate by workspace.** Each Linear account's entry shows *Workspace: {workspace}*, the Linear workspace that connection was granted. Two connections to different workspaces are separate accounts, so Kepler never reads one workspace's issues through another workspace's connection.

***

## Disconnect a provider

Click **Disconnect** on the provider's row in **Settings → Integrations** and confirm.

Disconnecting affects more than Kepler: it removes the connection from your GitKraken account, so the `gk` CLI and GitKraken Desktop lose it too. What happens to the provider depends on whether you have another account connected:

- **With another account connected**, Kepler promotes it to primary and the provider stays connected under it. Nothing else changes.
- **With no other account connected**, Kepler removes the provider entirely. Kepler drops its saved filters and its rows from your lists, so nothing in Kepler still points to a provider you no longer have.

You can reconnect at any time.

***

## Jira, Linear, and Trello have no pull requests

Kepler keeps 2 separate lists of what each provider can return: providers that can list issues, and providers that can list pull requests. Jira (Cloud, Server, and Data Center), Linear, and Trello are on the issues list only. As a result:

- **Kepler never asks them for pull requests.** Kepler leaves them out of the pull-request read instead of querying them and ignoring the result.
- **The interface hides filters that cannot match.** A provider filter only offers providers that can return results for what you are looking at, so Jira never appears as a pull-request filter. Kepler also builds the list's facets from the rows actually loaded, so a facet with nothing to match never appears.

The same rule applies the other way to Bitbucket and Bitbucket Data Center, which have no issues.

***

## What Kepler reads from an issue

When an issue becomes a task, Kepler attaches what it read, so the agent starts with that context instead of asking for it. Kepler reads these fields from the issue:

| Field | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Identifier** | The issue key or number: `GK-1234` for Jira, `DRE-2` for Linear, a number for GitHub, GitLab, and Azure DevOps |
| **Title** | |
| **Description** | The issue body. When an Azure DevOps work item keeps its content in another field, such as **Repro Steps** on a Bug, Kepler reads that field and labels the description with its name |
| **Issue type** | The provider's own vocabulary: a Jira issue type, an Azure DevOps work item type |
| **Author** | When the provider reports one |
| **Assignees** | |
| **Status** | The issue's current state, in the provider's own words (a Jira *To Verify* rather than a generic *open*), when the provider reports one |
| **Last updated** | When the issue was last updated |
| **Labels** | The provider's own labels, shown as badges in issue previews. Kepler distinguishes "this issue has no labels" from "this provider cannot report labels" |
| **Project or board** | Jira projects, Linear teams, Azure DevOps areas. Git hosts attach issues to a repository instead |
| **Iteration or sprint** | Azure DevOps iterations and Jira sprints. A Jira issue carried across sprints keeps them all |
| **Repository** | Name, owner, and host, for the git hosts |
| **URL** | Used by the open control, which names the provider: **Open on GitHub**, **Open on Jira**, and so on |

Kepler does not read an issue's priority field, due date, milestone, Trello checklist, or Linear cycle. An agent can still find these by opening the issue's URL itself, but Kepler does not deliver them as attached context. Todo's **Priority** grouping and filter come from labels instead: a label such as `P1`, `priority: high`, `blocker`, or `critical` sets the level, and the most urgent label wins. Jira and Linear keep priority in a field Kepler does not read, so their issues show as **Unprioritised** unless a label sets a priority. See [Arranging Your Work](/kepler/arranging-your-work).

Kepler converts descriptions to Markdown when the provider stores them in another format: Jira's wiki markup and Azure DevOps work items' HTML. Headings, code blocks, and tables then look the same in Kepler's previews and in the agent's context.

Images embedded in an issue's description, including Jira and Azure DevOps attachments, display in Kepler's issue previews. On a self-hosted server (GitHub Enterprise, GitLab Self-Hosted, Azure DevOps Server, or Jira Server / Data Center), these images are blocked and do not display, though the server's member avatars do. The agent receives the description as text: Kepler does not pass the attachments or images themselves.

### Comments

When you open an issue in a reader, either the task panel's side pane or the issue's pane on the task page, a **Comments** section under the summary shows its discussion. Kepler reads comments for **GitHub**, **GitHub Enterprise**, **GitLab**, **GitLab Self-Hosted**, **Jira**, and **Jira Server / Data Center**, through the same connection it reads the issue with. For other providers, the section says that comments for that provider are not available in Kepler yet.

Kepler reads up to the newest 100 comments, shows the latest ones with the newest at the bottom, and offers **Show earlier comments** for the rest it read. **Refresh comments** reads the discussion again. Each comment shows its author, when it was posted, and its body as Markdown. Comments are for you to read: Kepler shows them in the reader but does not attach them to the task or pass them to the agent.

### Which issues Kepler lists

Kepler lists open work. An issue that is finished or canceled in its tracker (a Linear issue in *Done* or *Canceled*, for example) leaves **Todo** and the issue pickers. An issue already attached to a task keeps showing on that task with its real state, finished or not.

**Todo** shows the issues related to you on each connected integration, across every organization you belong to. Each provider reports a different set of issues related to you:

| Provider | Issues Todo lists |
|---|---|
| **GitHub**, **GitHub Enterprise** | Yours, assigned to you, or mentioning you |
| **GitLab**, **GitLab Self-Hosted**, **Azure DevOps**, **Azure DevOps Server** | Yours or assigned to you |
| **Jira**, **Jira Server / Data Center**, **Linear**, **Trello** | Assigned to you |

An issue listed only because you were mentioned is marked **Mentioned**, so you can tell it apart from work that is yours. Hover the **Related to me** chip in Todo's header to see the rule for each integration you have connected.

To browse beyond that, use **All visible** in the issue list of **Add resources**. For GitHub and Azure DevOps, **All visible** reads every issue across your organizations, including repositories you can read outside them, such as ones where you are an outside collaborator. It loads more slowly. Jira and Linear show only your issues there until you pick a project or a team:

- **Jira**: when the issue list shows Jira alone, a project picker appears, starting with **All projects**. Pick a project to see every open issue in it. Kepler remembers the pick for each Jira connection.
- **Linear**: when the issue list shows Linear alone, a team picker and a **Project** picker appear. Pick a team, a Linear project, or both, to see every open issue in them, whoever it is assigned to. The **Project** picker starts at **All projects** and lists your Linear workspace's projects by name with their state (**Backlog**, **Planned**, **Started**, **Paused**, **Completed**, or **Canceled**), closed ones included. A Linear project can span teams, so the two pickers narrow together. Changing the team clears the project pick.

**A Linear issue synced with GitHub shows once.** When Linear's GitHub Issues sync keeps a two-way copy of a Linear issue on GitHub, Kepler pairs the 2 and lists them as one row, the Linear issue, with filter counts to match. In the GitHub copy's own panel, the copy is listed on its own again. The pair shares one task history, so a task started from either copy is the issue's task, whichever copy you look at.

When you start work from the Linear issue, Kepler uses the repository of its GitHub copy if exactly one repository you have in Kepler matches it. Otherwise, the Linear issue's own repository choice applies. Kepler pairs a copy only on GitHub or GitHub Enterprise Cloud that you are connected to, never on GitHub Enterprise Server. Pairing is also one-to-one only: Kepler does not pair a Linear issue synced with several GitHub issues, or 2 Linear issues that claim the same copy.

***

## Where your issues turn up

Your issues appear in 3 places:

| Surface | What it gives you |
|---|---|
| [The Kepler interface](/kepler/kepler-interface) | The **Todo** segment lists your issues across every connected tracker, grouped and filtered how you like |
| [Actions](/kepler/actions) | The **Action** button on a row hands the issue to an agent with its context attached. Running an Action on an issue that has no task also turns it into a task |
| [Tasks and Resources](/kepler/tasks-and-resources) | An issue is a resource on a task, so you can attach one to work that already exists |

The **Issue type**, **Label**, **Project**, and **Status** filters use your provider's own terms, not Kepler's. Azure DevOps and Jira issues also filter by **Iteration** and **Sprint**, each named the way its tracker names it.

Kepler recognizes an issue from its URL when you paste or attach one, including these work item URLs:

- **GitLab** work items, at `/-/work_items/<number>` in a project. Kepler stores them as issues of that project. A group-level work item belongs to no repository, so it stays a plain URL.
- **Azure DevOps** work items, at `/<organization>/<project>/_workitems/edit/<number>` or at the organization level, `/<organization>/_workitems/edit/<number>`.

**Search by key or link.** In the issue list of **Add resources**, type a Jira or Linear issue key, such as `OPS-42`, or paste a Jira Cloud, Jira Server / Data Center, Linear, or Azure DevOps work item link. Kepler looks that issue up directly from its tracker, whatever its state, rather than only filtering the rows already loaded. A Jira Server / Data Center link resolves when it points at an installation you have connected.

**Jira keys in commits and branches.** With Jira or Jira Server / Data Center connected, Kepler matches issue keys in commit messages and branch names against your Jira sites' own key patterns, so `OPS-42` in a commit message links to that issue. Right-click a commit in a worktree's commit list for **Open issue {issue}** and **Copy issue URL for {issue}** (see [Review Changes](/kepler/review-changes#the-changes-panel)), and the **Worktrees and branches** page shows the keys as chips on branch and worktree rows (see [Settings](/kepler/settings-repositories#worktrees-and-branches)). When 2 connected sites share a key, the label adds the site's address. Only Jira keys are linked this way; Kepler does not link other trackers' issue references in a commit.

**Pick from the list with the keyboard.** The issue list in **Add resources** has a preview pane and keyboard picking: arrows move between rows, **Space** selects, and **Enter** or a double-click adds. See [Picking issues and pull requests](/kepler/tasks-and-resources#picking-issues-and-pull-requests).

**Paste a link on the Links tab.** An issue URL pasted on the **Links** tab of **Add resources** is looked up and added as that issue, with **Add as plain link** to keep it a plain link. See [Pasting an issue link](/kepler/tasks-and-resources#pasting-an-issue-link).

**Paste a link into a prompt.** Paste an issue or pull request URL into a session's or a new task's composer and it becomes a link chip, which Kepler attaches to the task when you send. See [Sending a prompt](/kepler/agent-sessions#sending-a-prompt).

---

---
# Pull Request Integrations
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/pull-request-integrations/
product: Kepler
feature: Pull Request Integrations
content_type: how-to
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-10

Connect a Git host to see the pull requests you authored, and the ones waiting on your review, in [the Kepler interface](/kepler/kepler-interface). Kepler also matches each pull request to your existing worktrees, so a branch you are working on shows its pull request wherever the branch appears.

You manage providers in the **Issues and pull requests** section of **Settings → Integrations**.

Each connected Git host has a visibility line under its row. The line reads **Everything visible**, or shows how many items you have hidden. To leave organizations or repositories out of Todo, the lists, and the pickers, click **Choose what's visible…**. See [Choose what Kepler brings in](/kepler/issue-tracker-integrations#choose-what-kepler-brings-in).

***

## Hosts Kepler can read pull requests from

Of Kepler's 12 providers, 8 return pull requests:

| Provider | Also returns issues |
|---|---|
| **GitHub** | Yes |
| **GitHub Enterprise** | Yes |
| **GitLab** | Yes |
| **GitLab Self-Hosted** | Yes |
| **Azure DevOps** | Yes |
| **Azure DevOps Server** | Yes |
| **Bitbucket** | No |
| **Bitbucket Data Center** | No |

The other 4 providers (Jira, Jira Server / Data Center, Linear, and Trello) return issues only. See [Issue Tracker Integrations](/kepler/issue-tracker-integrations).

Kepler supports self-hosted instances. **GitHub Enterprise**, **GitLab Self-Hosted**, **Azure DevOps Server**, and **Bitbucket Data Center** read pull requests and merge requests the same way their cloud counterparts do, and 2 servers of the same kind stay separate. Which fields come back depends on your server's version.

You connect a self-hosted instance inside Kepler with its address and a personal access token, and Kepler checks the token against the server from your machine. See [Connect a self-hosted instance](#connect-a-self-hosted-instance). The instance must be reachable both from your machine and from gitkraken.dev, so you cannot connect a server that is only reachable inside your network or VPN.  Kepler trusts the certificates in your operating system's certificate store, so a server signed by your company's own certificate authority works without extra setup.

Kepler shows GitLab merge requests as pull requests, in the same list.

***

## Connect a Git host

To connect a cloud Git host (**GitHub**, **GitLab**, **Bitbucket**, or **Azure DevOps**), follow these steps:

1. Open **Settings → Integrations**.
2. Find the provider in **Issues and pull requests** and click **Connect**.
3. Authorize Kepler in the browser window that opens.
4. Return to Kepler, where the provider shows a **Connected** badge in **Issues and pull requests**.

Integrations belong to your GitKraken account, not to this copy of Kepler, so a provider you connect here is also available to the `gk` command-line interface (CLI) and GitKraken Desktop. To manage integrations, sign in to a GitKraken account.

For a cloud host, **Connect** sends you to GitKraken's website to authorize. Kepler opens `/connect` there in your system browser, names the provider, and includes a redirect back into Kepler. When you return, Kepler fetches your providers again instead of reusing its cached list.

While you authorize, Kepler keeps a **Connect {provider} in your browser** dialog open, with the provider's name in place of {provider}. If your browser did not open, copy the **Connection link** from the dialog and open it in a browser yourself. **Try again** makes a new link, because each link works once.

The dialog closes by itself as soon as the new connection appears, and Kepler checks for it again whenever you come back to a Kepler window. If Kepler cannot start the connection, the dialog reads **Unable to connect {provider}** and says why. **Reconnect** uses the same dialog.

### Connect a self-hosted instance

**GitHub Enterprise**, **GitLab Self-Hosted**, **Azure DevOps Server**, and **Bitbucket Data Center** connect inside Kepler with a personal access token rather than through the browser:

1. Open **Settings → Integrations**.
2. Find the provider in **Issues and pull requests** and click **Connect**. The **Connect {name}** dialog opens.
3. In **Server URL**, enter the server's address, including the port and installation path when your server uses them.
4. In **Personal access token**, paste a token with access to the repositories you need.
5. Click **Save connection**.

Kepler accepts only an `http` or `https` address without credentials, a query, or a fragment. It checks the token against the server from your machine, keeps it in a protected credential store on this device, and syncs the connection to your GitKraken account. The dialog reports how the check went:

| Message | What it means |
|---|---|
| *Credentials verified with the server.* | The server accepted the token |
| *Credentials saved. Unable to verify the server certificate. Check its TLS configuration.* | Kepler saved the token but could not verify the server's certificate |
| *Credentials saved without verification. Unable to reach the server.* | Kepler saved the token without checking it |
| *The server refused this token. Check its value and permissions.* | Fix the token and save again |

Until Kepler finishes syncing the connection to your account, the provider's row shows **Cloud sync pending**, and you cannot make that connection the primary. If Kepler cannot reach GitKraken, it retries when you refresh your providers. **Reconnect** on a self-hosted provider opens the same dialog, so you can replace an expired or rejected token there.

Use these controls to manage connected providers:

| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Reconnect** | Runs authorization again. Use it when a sign-in has expired |
| **Disconnect** | Removes the provider. See [Disconnect a provider](#disconnect-a-provider) |
| **Refresh** | At the top of the section, checks every provider again |

A provider's row can show a warning:

- **Sign-in expired**: the token needs refreshing. Kepler tries to refresh it by itself; **Reconnect** refreshes it by hand.
- **Cannot connect to server**: the integration is still connected, but Kepler could not reach the server. Instead of reconnecting, check that the server is up and reachable from your network or VPN.
- An organization named under the row: that organization refuses Kepler's access, such as a GitHub organization that restricts OAuth apps. Kepler leaves out only that organization's items.

See [Issue Tracker Integrations](/kepler/issue-tracker-integrations) for the warnings in full.

***

## Cloning a repository for a pull request

When you start work on a pull request from a repository you have never cloned, Kepler first clones the repository into your **Default Repositories Folder**. The clone authenticates with the provider token that your connected GitKraken account already holds, the same connection the pull request came through. As a result, a private repository clones without you having to set up a Git credential helper. How the clone authenticates depends on the host:

| Host | How the clone authenticates |
|---|---|
| **GitHub**, **GitHub Enterprise** | Your connected account's token |
| **GitLab**, **GitLab Self-Hosted** | Your connected account's token |
| **Bitbucket**, **Bitbucket Data Center**, **Azure DevOps**, **Azure DevOps Server** | Your own Git credentials |

For an enterprise or self-managed host, Kepler matches the clone's host against the domain stored on your connection. The repository then clones through the account connected to that instance, not through a cloud account from the same vendor. When a provider has more than one account, the clone uses the account Kepler reads from: **Read from this account** where you set one, otherwise the primary.

Kepler passes the token only to that one Git process. Kepler does not write the token into the clone's `.git/config` or add it to the remote's URL, and never shows it in the interface.

If Kepler has no usable token for the host, the clone uses your own Git credential helper. Kepler never lets Git open an interactive prompt, so when no credential helper is available, the clone fails with a message that names the host and tells you what to do: *git has no saved credentials for this remote and Kepler cannot prompt for them. Sign in with a git credential helper (e.g. `gh auth login`, or the macOS keychain helper) or use an SSH url, then try again.*

***

## More than one account of the same provider

You can connect several accounts of the same provider. When a provider has two or more, an **Accounts** list appears under its row with one entry per account.

Each entry carries two independent controls:

| Control | What it changes | How far it reaches |
|---|---|---|
| **Read from this account** | Which account Kepler reads this provider's pull requests and issues from | Kepler only, and non-destructive |
| **Set as primary** / **Primary** | The provider's primary account | Everywhere: other Kepler windows, the `gk` CLI, and GitKraken Desktop |

**Browsing a secondary account does not change your primary.** Selecting **Read from this account** on a second account switches what Kepler shows you and leaves the primary alone. The primary is the default read account, so a provider with no override reads through it.

Changing either one clears that provider's saved filters, because a repository from the old account might not exist on the new one. Kepler then fetches the list again.

***

## Disconnect a provider

Click **Disconnect** on the provider's row in **Settings → Integrations** and confirm.

Disconnecting affects more than Kepler: it removes the connection from your GitKraken account, so the `gk` CLI and GitKraken Desktop lose it too. What happens to the provider depends on whether you have another account connected:

- **With another account connected**, Kepler promotes it to primary and the provider stays connected under it. Nothing else changes.
- **With no other account connected**, Kepler removes the provider entirely. Kepler drops its saved filters and its rows from your lists, so nothing in Kepler still points to a provider you no longer have.

You can reconnect at any time.

***

## Bitbucket has no issues

Kepler keeps 2 separate lists of what each provider can return: providers that can list issues, and providers that can list pull requests. Bitbucket and Bitbucket Data Center are on the pull-request list only, so Kepler never asks them for issues, and a provider filter for issues never offers them. Kepler also builds the list's facets from the rows actually loaded, so a facet with nothing to match never appears.

The same rule applies the other way to Jira, Linear, and Trello, which have no pull requests.

***

## How pull requests attach to worktrees

Kepler matches a pull request to a worktree by **branch**. It tries the worktree's **upstream branch** as well as its local one.

The upstream pass matters when the 2 names differ. If your local branch is `fix-login` but it tracks `origin/justin/fix-login`, the pull request's head branch is the upstream name, so matching on the local name alone finds nothing. Kepler's second pass compares against the short branch name of the tracking ref and finds the match.

Matching covers open and closed pull requests together, so a merged pull request still shows on the branch it merged from.

### Confirmed and inferred links

Kepler records **how** it made each link, so you can tell a confirmed link from a guess:

| How the link was made | Reads as | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| Recorded on the task | Confirmed | The link is authoritative. Kepler records one when you launch the task from the pull request, when an agent opens a pull request, when you attach one yourself, or through the branch auto-attach below |
| The pull request's head branch matched the worktree's local branch | Confirmed | A direct branch match |
| The head branch matched the worktree branch's **upstream** branch | Confirmed, and marked | Git-native rather than a guess, but the local name differs, so Kepler labels it **Matched from upstream branch** |
| An identifier parsed out of the branch name | Inferred | A heuristic. Issues only: pull requests are never linked this way |

A confirmed link has no extra marking. Kepler draws a dotted underline under any link you should check, and its tooltip says why: **Matched from upstream branch**, or **Matched from branch name** for an inferred issue link.

When Kepler finds the same pull request in more than one way, the most authoritative link wins: the task's own recorded link, then a local branch match, then an upstream branch match.

Kepler matches branches only within each item's own repository, so a pull request in one repository never matches a branch of the same name in another.

### Auto-attaching a matched pull request

When you open a pull request outside Kepler (with `gh` in a terminal, from GitKraken Desktop, or on the web), Kepler records it on the task for you, instead of only matching it each time it reads your pull requests.

Whenever new pull-request data arrives, Kepler checks your active tasks that have no pull request yet, and attaches one whose head branch matches a worktree's branch. The pull request then behaves like one you attached yourself: it appears in the task's resources, and the agent receives it as context. See [Tasks and Resources](/kepler/tasks-and-resources).

Auto-attach is stricter than branch matching, because Kepler saves an attached resource and sends it to an agent, while a match only shows a card. Auto-attach follows 4 rules:

| Rule | Why |
|---|---|
| Exact matches only | The pull request's head branch has to be the worktree's own branch name, and its repository has to match a remote exactly. The upstream-branch pass and the rename-tolerant fallback still show the card; neither attaches |
| Open pull requests only | A merged pull request cannot claim a branch name that gets reused later |
| The head branch has to live in the same repository | Branch matching keys on the head branch name, and the author of a fork picks that name freely. An attached resource reaches your agent, so a stranger's pull request must not claim your branch |
| One pull request per task per pass | A task drops out of the next pass as soon as it holds one |

Auto-attach still attaches a pull request that another active task already holds, because several active tasks can share one pull request. Attaching it to one task leaves it on the other, and restoring an archived task that holds it archives nothing.

Auto-attach never archives or replaces anything. A branch match is a guess, so it never replaces work you started on purpose, and it never removes a link because a pull request was briefly missing from a read.

***

## What Kepler reads from a pull request

Kepler reads these fields from a pull request:

| Field | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Number and title** | |
| **Description** | The pull request body |
| **State** | Kepler derives one of **Open**, **Draft**, **Merged**, or **Closed** |
| **Repository** | Name, owner, and host |
| **Author** | When the provider reports one. Kepler also tracks whether you authored it, which decides whether a row shows **Yours** or **Review** |
| **Head and base branch** | When the provider reports them. These drive branch matching and the branch a task starts from |
| **Fork** | Whether the head branch lives on a fork, and where, so Kepler can fetch it from the fork remote instead of `origin` |
| **Created at** | |
| **URL** | Used by the open control, which names the provider: **Open on GitHub**, **Open on Bitbucket**, and so on |

A merged pull request keeps its description and author for as long as a task, archived or not, still links it.

On a self-hosted server (GitHub Enterprise, GitLab Self-Hosted, Azure DevOps Server, or Bitbucket Data Center), images embedded in a pull request's description are blocked and do not display in Kepler's previews. The server's member avatars still load.

Azure DevOps reports pull requests without a usable number, so Kepler identifies them by URL instead. You do not see a difference, and identifying by URL is why a pull request you look up by link resolves correctly there.

***

## Where your pull requests turn up

Your pull requests appear in 4 places:

| Surface | What it gives you |
|---|---|
| [The Kepler interface](/kepler/kepler-interface) | The **Todo** segment lists the pull requests related to you on each connected host, with your role on each |
| [Actions](/kepler/actions) | The **Action** button hands the pull request to an agent. **Review** and **Address Feedback** are the 2 built-in Actions for pull requests, and Kepler picks one based on who authored the pull request |
| [Review Changes](/kepler/review-changes) | Reading the diff and the commits behind a pull request |
| [Tasks and Resources](/kepler/tasks-and-resources) | A pull request is a resource on a task, so you can attach one to work that already exists |

**Todo's scope differs by host.** Each provider reports a different set of pull requests related to you, so Todo lists these from each:

| Host | Pull requests Todo lists |
|---|---|
| **GitHub**, **GitHub Enterprise** | Yours, assigned to you, or ones you review |
| **GitLab**, **GitLab Self-Hosted**, **Azure DevOps**, **Azure DevOps Server**, **Bitbucket Data Center** | Yours or awaiting your review |
| **Bitbucket** | Yours, or awaiting your review in your workspaces and repositories added to Kepler |

Hover the **Related to me** chip in Todo's header to see the rule for each integration you have connected. See [Issue Tracker Integrations](/kepler/issue-tracker-integrations#which-issues-kepler-lists) for the issue side.

**Review requests come from every host.** Pull requests waiting on your review show up from Azure DevOps, Azure DevOps Server, and Bitbucket Data Center as well as GitHub and GitLab. Bitbucket Cloud has no account-wide way to ask for them, so Kepler reads review requests repository by repository, starting with the repositories you have in Kepler and then the rest of your workspaces at a pace that stays inside Bitbucket's hourly request limits. On a large workspace they can take a while to appear.

**Kepler loads the lists you are looking at.** Pull request and issue lists refresh while they are on screen, and again when you come back to the window, instead of downloading your whole account's lists in the background. A task's own pull requests refresh when an agent ends a turn, a branch is pushed, or a pull request is published. When one provider fails to load, the others keep loading, and the failed provider's last loaded pull requests stay in the list.

**A failing provider is named, with its fix.** When a connected provider's read fails, Todo, the **Add resources** lists, and a link preview show a warning that names the provider and what went wrong, such as *GitHub needs you to sign in again, so its work may be missing.* On Todo the warning sits under **Unable to load your work**. Each warning offers one fix:

| What went wrong | The fix offered |
|---|---|
| The sign-in needs renewing | **Reconnect**, or **Reconnect in settings** for a self-hosted provider, which needs a new token |
| The provider refused part of the request, so some organizations or repositories may be missing | **Open settings** |
| Rate limiting, an unreachable server, an unreadable answer, or a temporary problem | **Retry** |

Rows kept from the last good load show a cloud mark on their provider chip, labeled *Not refreshed: shown from the last successful {provider} load.*

**The pull request picker says why its list is empty.** When you attach a pull request from **Add resources**, the picker explains an empty list instead of showing *No matches*:

- If the **Linked work** filter hides pull requests, the picker says how many it hides and which filter hides them, and offers **Show all**.
- If no connected provider can list pull requests, the picker reads **Connect your code host** and lists the providers that can fill the tab, each with **Connect**.

The **Linked work** filter defaults to **No active task**. A task counts as active until you archive it, so Done and on-hold tasks count. The filter has 5 options:

| Option | Shows pull requests |
|---|---|
| **Any** | Whatever their task history |
| **No active task** | With no task, or with archived tasks only. This default keeps earlier work easy to find, so you do not duplicate it |
| **No tasks ever** | Never linked to a task |
| **Has an active task** | Linked to at least one task that is not archived |
| **Archived tasks only** | Linked only to archived tasks |

A row with task history carries a badge: **Task** or **{count} tasks** when one of them is active, **Archived task** or **{count} archived tasks** when all are archived.

When nothing you have connected can list issues or pull requests, **Add resources** opens on a connect view, **Connect where your work lives**, with a tile for each provider. Connect each one you use, then click **Continue**. The provider filter's menu also offers **Connect another provider…**, which opens the same view with a **Back** button.

You can also start work on a pull request from GitLens or GitKraken Desktop. See [Create a task](/kepler/create-task).

---
