# Settings
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/settings/
product: Kepler
feature: Settings
content_type: reference
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-10

Use Settings to change how Kepler, your agents, and your tasks work. Settings has 15 pages. For what each setting on a page does, its default, and what changes when you change it, open that page's reference from [The Settings pages](#the-settings-pages).

To open Settings, click the gear icon in the top bar, or press **⌘ ,** (**Ctrl ,** on Windows and Linux). To close it, click the gear icon or press the same shortcut again.

***

## The Settings pages

The Settings sidebar, down the left of Settings, starts with a **Search settings** field and [**Setup**](/kepler/settings-setup-account#setup), a progress ring that reopens the first-run checklist. Below them, the sidebar lists the following pages, in this order:

| Page | What it covers |
|---|---|
| [**Account**](/kepler/settings-setup-account#account) | Who you're signed in as, your organization, what your plan unlocks, and GitKraken AI credits |
| [**Agents**](/kepler/settings-agents) | Your agents, custom agents, MCP servers, agent tools, approvals, and usage limits |
| [**Tasks**](/kepler/settings-tasks) | How new tasks start, including the default agent and the agent new sessions start with, and how a task's page looks |
| [**Repositories**](/kepler/settings-repositories) | The repositories folder, your repos and folders, worktrees and branches, and Projects |
| [**Integrations**](/kepler/settings-integrations) | Issue tracker and Git host connections, and sessions started in your own terminal |
| [**Actions**](/kepler/settings-actions) | Preferred Actions per item kind, and the Action list |
| [**General**](/kepler/settings-app#general) | Language, windows, the default editor, and keeping agents running |
| [**Notifications**](/kepler/settings-app#notifications) | Which agent events notify you, on the desktop and in Kepler |
| [**Appearance**](/kepler/settings-app#appearance) | Light or dark appearance and themes, the chat, the terminal font, code font size, and diff layout |
| [**Voice input**](/kepler/settings-app#voice-input) | On-device speech-to-text, its transcription engine, and learned words |
| [**Keyboard shortcuts**](/kepler/settings-app#keyboard-shortcuts) | Kepler's keyboard shortcuts |
| [**Remote environments**](/kepler/settings-environment#remote-environments) | The machines your agents can run on, over SSH or WSL |
| [**Remote Access**](/kepler/settings-environment#remote-access) | Opening this Kepler from another device |
| [**Updates**](/kepler/settings-updates-help#updates) | The installed version and app updates |
| [**Help**](/kepler/settings-updates-help#help) | The docs, release notes, onboarding guides, and Kepler's logs |

**Account** is the only page about you rather than the app. The account menu opens it.

### Find a setting

To find a setting by name, type in **Search settings**. Search matches section titles, control labels, help text, and common synonyms, so a word like *theme* or *notifications* finds the right section. With no match, the results read *No settings match "{query}"*.

To go straight to one setting, type `@id:` followed by its id, such as `@id:terminal.font-size`. Case does not matter. The results show that one setting under its page and section. Choose it to open the page on that control. If this version of Kepler has no setting with that id, the results read *No setting has that id.* [Settings links](#deep-links-and-section-anchors) use the same ids.

Ask Kepler and your agents can also search Kepler's settings, and change one when you ask. They link you to a setting with a [settings link](#deep-links-and-section-anchors). Some changes need your approval first. Settings that hold secrets, such as your account or integrations, can only be linked. See [Finding and changing settings](/kepler/ask-kepler#finding-and-changing-settings).

To jump to a section, use the section links the Settings sidebar shows under the page you have open. Under **Agents**, the sidebar also lists each supported agent below **Your agents**. A page with fewer than 2 listed sections shows no section links.

### Sub-pages and unsaved changes

When you open an item to edit it, such as a repository, a project, a custom agent, an MCP server, or an Action, it opens as a sub-page inside its Settings page, with a breadcrumb back to the page.

If you leave a sub-page with unsaved changes, Kepler asks before it discards anything. It asks however you leave: **Escape**, **Back**, the form's own **Cancel**, a page in the Settings sidebar, or a link elsewhere in the app:

- A form that can save asks **Save your changes?**, with **Cancel**, **Don't save**, and **Save**.
- A form that has nothing to save yet, such as a step-by-step add flow, asks **Discard your changes?**, with **Keep editing** and **Discard**.

A form with a **Save** button keeps it in a footer with **Cancel**. While you have unsaved edits, the footer reads *Unsaved changes*. If a save fails, the footer shows why and keeps your edits on the form. When a save succeeds, Kepler confirms with *Saved {name}*.

Most fields outside those forms save themselves. Each one shows its own status beside it: **Saving**, **Saved**, or **Unable to save** with the reason. A switch shows only **Saving** and a failure. If a save fails after you've left the page, Kepler tells you which setting it was: *Unable to save {label}*.

**Back**, or your mouse's back button, steps back through each page, sub-page, and search result you opened in Settings. To leave Settings in one click from any page or sub-page, use the back arrow in the Settings header, the gear icon, or **⌘ ,** (**Ctrl ,**). Each one returns you to what you were doing before you opened Settings.

### Settings in a remote window

In a window connected to a remote environment, Settings shows that machine's settings, and its header names the machine. Under its title, each page says where its settings are saved:

- **Saved on {machine}**: on the remote machine.
- **Saved on this machine**: on your own computer. Its tooltip reads *Applies to every Kepler window on this machine, whichever machine it's connected to.*

A section that saves somewhere other than its page has its own badge. To change this machine's own settings from a remote window, click **Open this machine's settings** in the header. The same page opens in a local window.

Some settings are kept on your own computer, such as the language, the default editor, the themes, the terminal and code fonts, and the diff layout. When Ask Kepler or an agent in a remote window changes one of these, the window applies the change on your computer, the same as its Settings page would. A notification names the change, with **Undo**. See [Finding and changing settings](/kepler/ask-kepler#finding-and-changing-settings).

### Deep links and section anchors

Every section has a stable anchor id. A link of the form `/settings/<page>#<section-id>` opens that page and scrolls to the section.

`/settings` on its own opens the last page that window had open, or **Agents** if it had none. Older links of the form `/settings#<section-id>` still work: Kepler finds the page that owns that section and keeps the hash. An id that no page owns anymore, such as `general`, `windows-and-notifications`, `keyboard-shortcuts`, or `features`, opens **Agents**.

The following table lists each page's path with its section anchors, in page order:

| Page path | Section anchors, in page order |
|---|---|
| `/settings/account` | `account`, `plan-features`, `ai-credits` |
| `/settings/agents` | `agents`, `ask-kepler`, `custom-agents`, `mcp-servers`, `agent-git-tools`, `approvals`, `usage-limits` |
| `/settings/tasks` | `new-tasks`, `default-agent`, `task-page` |
| `/settings/repositories` | `repositories-root`, `repositories`, `worktrees`, `projects` |
| `/settings/integrations` | `provider-integrations`, `agent-options` |
| `/settings/actions` | `preferred-actions`, `action-list` |
| `/settings/general` | `language`, `windows`, `default-editor`, `keep-running` |
| `/settings/notifications` | `system-notifications` |
| `/settings/appearance` | `appearance`, `transcript`, `terminal`, `code`, `diff-view` |
| `/settings/voice` | `voice`, `voice-engine`, `voice-dictation`, `voice-learned` |
| `/settings/keyboard-shortcuts` | `shortcuts-general`, `shortcuts-navigation`, `shortcuts-dashboard`, `shortcuts-task-page`, `shortcuts-chat`, `shortcuts-changes` |
| `/settings/remote-environments` | `remote-environments`, `found-machines`, `remote-windows` |
| `/settings/remote-access` | `remote-access` |
| `/settings/updates` | `updates` |
| `/settings/help` | `onboarding-help`, `logs` |

A few anchors work differently, and some items have anchors of their own:

- `default-agent` is inside **New tasks**, not a section of its own.
- `ask-kepler` is not a section of its own either. It marks the default agent picker for Ask Kepler at the top of the [Agents page](/kepler/settings-agents).
- From the Settings sidebar or search, `worktrees` opens the **Worktrees and branches** sub-page instead of scrolling to its row.
- Each agent has an anchor on the Agents page, `agent-<agent-id>`, for example `agent-claude-code`. Each custom agent has `custom-agent-row-<id>`.
- Each setting's control has the anchor `setting-<id>`, where `<id>` is the setting's id, for example `/settings/appearance#setting-terminal.font-size`.

When search, a link, or a pointer on another page sends you to one setting, Kepler waits for its control to load, highlights it, and moves focus to it. The highlight then fades. If the control is in a collapsed part of the page, such as an agent's program and data folder, Kepler opens that part first. If the control does not appear, Kepler explains why instead:

- An agent setting the agent's card does not show reads *This agent shows that setting only when it is turned on and supports it.*
- A setting that depends on something else reads *This setting appears once what it depends on is set up.*
- Otherwise, Kepler fills **Search settings** with `@id:<id>`, so you can see where the setting lives.

#### Settings links

A `kepler://` link opens Settings from anywhere: another app, a terminal, or an agent's reply in Kepler, where it's clickable.

| Link | Opens |
|---|---|
| `kepler://settings` | Settings |
| `kepler://settings/<id>` | Settings on one setting's control, for example `kepler://settings/terminal.font-size` |

A setting id is a list of lowercase words separated by dots, and a link matches it in any case. A settings link only opens Settings: it never changes a setting, and a value added to the link is ignored. A link to an id this version of Kepler does not have opens Settings with *That setting isn't in this version of Kepler.*

---

# Setup and Account Settings
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/settings-setup-account/
product: Kepler
feature: Settings
content_type: reference
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-10

Use **Setup** to get back to Kepler's first-run checklist. Use **Account** to see who you are signed in as, which organization you are acting as, what your plan includes, and how you are using your GitKraken AI credits.

## Setup

To reopen the first-run checklist, click **Setup** at the top of the Settings sidebar, under **Search settings**. Its progress ring shows how much of the checklist is done. For what the checklist asks you to do, and how to hide it from the toolbar, see [Getting Started → Finish the setup checklist](/kepler/kepler-getting-started#finish-the-setup-checklist).

***

## Account

The **Account** page has these controls:

| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Account** | Who you are signed in as, with your name and email |
| Organization | Your active organization and its plan. If your GitKraken account belongs to more than 1 organization, this line is a switcher |
| **Refresh account status** | Reads your plan again. Kepler also picks up a purchase or plan change you make outside the app by itself, without a restart |
| **Manage account** / **Manage subscription** | Opens your GitKraken account or subscription on gitkraken.dev |
| **Unlock more with Kepler** | What this plan includes and what it does not. Shown only while something is left to unlock |
| **GitKraken AI credits** | Your credit balance, with **Buy credits**, and **Your usage by feature**. Shown only when there is a balance to show |

The organization you are acting as decides what a feature costs and whether it is unlocked at all.

**Your usage by feature** shows where your AI credits went. It appears once you have used an AI feature. A stacked bar splits your use between your 3 most-used AI features and everything else, shown as **Other**. Below the bar, each feature has a row with its share of your use as a percentage, such as **Commit Message**, **Conflict Resolution**, **Compose Changes**, or **Task & branch names**. To see what a feature does, hover its help icon.

### When a feature is locked

If a feature is locked on the organization you are acting as but included on another organization you belong to, Kepler offers to switch instead of showing a paywall: *{organization} ({plan}) already includes this.*, with **Switch to organization**.

If you just changed your plan, use **Check again** under **Already upgraded?** on the paywall. If nothing has changed, the paywall reads *Still on {plan}*. A paywall that covers the whole window also shows an account card with **Signed in as**, your **Current organization**, and a **Switch** button for each other organization whose plan includes the feature.

### Trials

When a trial starts, a dialog reads **You just opened up all of Kepler**, with a pill that shows how many days are free (*{count} days free*). It lists what the trial unlocks: *Every feature below is yours until {date}.*

When the trial ends, a dialog reads **Your trial has ended** and lists **What your trial included**. It offers an upgrade or, if your account can start the trial again, a way to continue where you stopped.

---

---
# Agent Settings
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/settings-agents/
product: Kepler
feature: Settings
content_type: reference
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-10

Use **Settings → Agents** to install and update the coding agents that work on your tasks, sign in to them, choose how each one starts, and give them more tools.

At the top of the page, a line names the agent new tasks use: *New tasks use {agent}.* or *No default agent for new tasks.* To change it, click **Change in Tasks**, which opens [Default agent](/kepler/settings-tasks#default-agent).

To choose the agent Ask Kepler uses, set the **Ask Kepler uses** row. This **Ask Kepler default agent** is separate from the default for tasks. Its help text reads *Used when Ask Kepler has no earlier pick to go on and whenever you choose Use default agent there.* The row lists only the agents that can answer in the Ask Kepler panel, which are the agents that run in **Chat**. If the agent you picked stops being available, the row reads *Pick another agent for Ask Kepler: {name} is not available.* See [Ask Kepler](/kepler/ask-kepler#which-agents-can-answer).

## Your agents

Kepler supports **Claude Code**, **Codex**, **GitHub Copilot**, **OpenCode**, **Pi**, **Auggie**, **Antigravity**, **Cursor**, and **Grok Build**. Settings lists the agents installed on this machine first, then the rest, each group in that order.

In the section header, **Update all** runs each installed agent's own updater, and **Re-scan** looks again for the agent CLIs installed on this machine. If you install or remove an agent outside Kepler, click **Re-scan**.

Each agent has a card. The card's title line shows the agent's name and these controls:

| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| Version | The installed version, or **Not installed** when Kepler cannot find the CLI. **Version unknown**, in a warning tone, means Kepler could not read the version |
| **Update** | Runs the agent's updater and streams its output. Shown when Kepler has an updater for that agent |
| **Install** | Runs an installer for you and streams the output. Shown on an agent that is not installed and has an installer for your OS. **Cancel** stops an install in progress: *Install cancelled: {name}* |
| **Enabled** | *Off keeps it installed but hidden when you start work.* |

When the version is unknown, Kepler turns off features that depend on the version, such as sending a new session's first message automatically. Reinstalling or updating the agent usually fixes this.

If the installed version of an agent, or of one of its components, has a known problem, a warning note appears on the card under the title line. The note names the version and says what to do. Kepler can show these notes:

| Note | What it means |
|---|---|
| *OpenCode {version} is not supported* | Sessions with this version do not start. Install OpenCode 2, or choose an OpenCode 2 binary under **Program and data folder** |
| *Auggie {version} may not load your MCP servers in chat* | Kepler's fix for how Auggie loads MCP servers covers only the Auggie versions it was built for |
| *ACP server {version} can fail to start on Linux* | Antigravity's Chat server can be killed at startup on some Linux systems. Reinstall it under **Program and data folder** |
| *Codex {version} can show approval prompts that need no answer* | Update Codex to 0.163.0 or newer |

The card body holds the rest:

| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Accounts** | Runs more than 1 login for the agent side by side. Available for Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot, Auggie, and Grok Build. See [Use several accounts for one agent](#use-several-accounts-for-one-agent) |
| **Account** | On an agent with a single login: who is signed in, with **Sign in** or **Sign out**. Signing out deletes the stored credentials |
| **New sessions start in** | The default mode for new sessions. See below |
| **Artifacts in new sessions** | Claude Code only. See below |
| **Let artifact comments start turns** | Claude Code only. See below |
| **Program and data folder** | A disclosure holding **Binary**, **Components**, and **Data folder** |

Under **Program and data folder**:

| Setting | What it controls | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **Binary** | The agent program Kepler runs. **Auto** finds it the way your shell does, as the first match on your `PATH`, so it matches `which`. To override it, pick a specific install or **Custom path…**, or click **Re-scan** to search again | Auto |
| **Components** | Extra pieces an agent can need, such as its CLI for Terminal mode (*Needed for Terminal mode.*), each with **Install** or **Update to {version}** | None |
| **Data folder** | *Overrides the agent's default data and config folder.* | Empty, meaning the agent's own default |

**Codex runs your own CLI.** Like every other agent, Kepler finds and runs the `codex` you have installed. For usage figures, Kepler reads the OAuth token from `~/.codex/auth.json`, or from `CODEX_HOME/auth.json` when you have set a custom data folder.

**OpenCode needs version 2.** Kepler reads and resumes only OpenCode 2's sessions. A session does not start on an OpenCode 1 binary, and the card shows *OpenCode {version} is not supported*. If you have both versions installed, point **Binary** at OpenCode 2. A conversation you started under OpenCode 1 resumes from OpenCode 2's copy of it.

**Antigravity runs in Chat through its Agent Client Protocol (ACP) server.** That server is a separate component from its `agy` terminal CLI. See [Agent Integrations](/kepler/agent-integrations).

### Use several accounts for one agent

With **Accounts**, you can run more than 1 login for an agent side by side. Each account has its own credentials and history, but shares your skills, agents, commands, and settings.

To add an account, click **Add account**, then choose whether its conversations **Keep separate** or **Share with the CLI**.

Each account row has the following controls:

- A color picker that tints the agent icon wherever that account runs. The default account stays uncolored, so its picker shows the ⊘ **No color** mark.
- **Sign in**.
- An account menu with **Rename**, **Share history with the CLI**, **Sign in another way**, **Sign out**, and **Remove account**. On a signed-in Claude Code account, the menu also has **Switch account…**, which signs that account in with a different Claude login. See [Switch the account a Claude Code login uses](#switch-the-account-a-claude-code-login-uses).

Removing an account stops its running sessions and deletes the sessions stored only in that account. To keep those sessions, click **Move to CLI account** first. See [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions#several-accounts-for-one-agent).

### When an added account stops sharing your settings

An added account shares your own settings, instructions, skills, agents, commands, and other configuration by linking to your files. If the agent saves a change while signed in to that account, the agent can write its own copy in place of the link. The account then stops following your file. Kepler shows this under the account's row: *This account stopped sharing your {items}*. Expand the message to see both paths, **This account's copy** and **Your {item}**, and choose one of the following:

- **Share your {item} again** asks first, then links the account back to your file. *Its own copy is saved as a backup next to it, so nothing is lost.*
- **Keep its own {item}** keeps the account's copy. The row's menu then offers **Share your {item} again** if you change your mind.

### Switch the account a Claude Code login uses

**Switch account…** opens **Switch the account for {name}?**, which names the login now signed in. *If your browser is already signed in, choose a different account on the sign-in page.* The dialog also warns you about the following:

- How many running sessions use the account, and when they pick up the new login: when they restart, or on their next request.
- On the default account, the one the CLI uses, the switch *also changes the account the claude command uses in your own terminals.*

**Continue** opens the usual sign-in. When the sign-in succeeds, Kepler confirms: *{name} is now signed in as {login}.*

### Default mode for new sessions

Every agent that can run in both Chat and Terminal has this setting:

| Setting | What it controls | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **New sessions start in** | **Chat**: *{agent} built into Kepler, with replies, diffs and plans you can read, review and search.* **Terminal**: *{agent}'s own command-line app, with its commands, shortcuts and settings, just as you use it today.* | Chat. Google Antigravity starts on Terminal, because its Chat server signs in separately |

Kepler saves the choice per agent, so one agent can default to Terminal while another stays on Chat. The setting is only a default. As its help text says, *You can pick the other one when you start a session.* A terminal-only agent shows **Terminal** with no switch. See [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions#how-a-session-runs).

### Artifacts in new sessions

The following setting is on Claude Code's card:

| Setting | What it controls | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **Artifacts in new sessions** | *The Artifact tools let the agent publish pages and designs. They add about 12k tokens to the context of every session that has them. Each session can still turn them on or off from its session menu.* | Off |

A running Chat session has its own **Artifacts** switch in its agent settings. When you turn it on, Kepler asks **Turn on Artifacts?**, then restarts the session and resumes the conversation. Once a conversation has artifacts on, they stay on for that conversation. See [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions).

### Let artifact comments start turns

The following setting is on Claude Code's card:

| Setting | What it controls | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **Let artifact comments start turns** | Anyone with edit access to an artifact a Chat session publishes can start a turn in that session by sending a comment to Claude. The session posts a reply automatically | On |

Running sessions keep the value they started with. When you change the setting, the card lists the sessions still on the previous value. It marks the sessions that **Published an artifact**, have a **Turn in progress**, or have **Background work running**. To apply the new value, click **Restart all** or **Restart selected ({count})**. A session that is mid-turn or has background work starts unticked.

Restarting keeps each conversation. It interrupts a turn in progress and stops background work, and a restarted session stops watching the artifacts it published before.

## Custom agents

To run an agent that Kepler does not list, add it as a custom agent by giving Kepler its command. To add one, click **New custom agent** in the section header. To edit one, click its row. Either way, the agent opens as a sub-page with these fields:

| Field | What it takes |
|---|---|
| **Name** | The name Kepler shows for the agent |
| **Command** | The program to run, for example `/usr/local/bin/my-agent` or `my-agent` |
| **Args (one per line)** | Arguments passed to the command |
| **Environment variables (KEY=value, one per line)** | Environment for the command |
| **Runs in** | **Chat**: *Kepler's chat. Needs a program that speaks ACP (the Agent Client Protocol).* **Terminal**: *The command's own app, in a terminal.* |

Custom agents appear with the built-in agents wherever you pick an agent. With none added, the section reads *No custom agents yet.*

Kepler encrypts environment values at rest and hides existing values when you edit an agent. To keep a stored secret, leave its value empty (`KEY=`). To replace it, type a new value.

**Save** waits until Kepler has stored the agent. If the save fails, the form stays open with the reason: *Unable to save {name}: {reason}*. **Delete** asks first, with **Delete custom agent?**: *Deletes {name} and the environment values stored with it.* You cannot undo a delete.

## MCP servers

Use **MCP servers** to give your agents extra tools, like a database, a browser, or your issue tracker. The servers here are each agent's own defaults, and every repository inherits them.

To see the servers an agent loads, pick the agent with **Agent**. If that agent has more than 1 account, pick an account too. Kepler lists only the agents that expose their MCP servers to Kepler. In the list:

- Click a server to open its own page. There you can turn the server or a single tool off, sign in to a server that needs it, use **Also add to…** to copy the server to another agent, and **Remove server**.
- Click **Add server** in the section header to add one.

A server or tool you turn off here is off in every repository, unless a repository turns it back on for itself. A repository's own **MCP servers** section is on its [Edit repo](/kepler/settings-repositories#edit-a-repository) page. See [MCP Servers](/kepler/mcp-servers).

Below the list, one more setting applies across every agent:

| Setting | What it controls | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **Keep the GitKraken MCP server installed in every agent** | *Gives every command-line agent Git tools and your issues and pull requests through GitKraken. Turn off to manage it yourself.* | On |

This setting affects the MCP clients on your machine. Separately, Kepler attaches its own workspace MCP server to every session it starts. The workspace MCP server is always on and has no setting. Its tools are named for what they act on, such as `task_get`, `session_start`, or `worktree_create`. They let the agent:

- Read a task and its resources, find tasks, create a task, change its Progress stage, name, or hold, and archive it.
- Read, write, and delete the task's notes.
- Attach and detach issue, pull request, and URL links, and attach or detach files.
- List the agents, repositories, and folders in your workspace. An agent can name a repository by one of its [aliases](/kepler/settings-repositories#edit-a-repository).
- Create, attach, detach, update, or delete one of the task's worktrees.
- List and read sessions, start a session with the agent it chooses, send follow-ups, rename or archive a session, and read the reports its own sessions send back.
- List pending approvals.
- Read and save themes. See [Theme](/kepler/settings-app#theme).
- Rebase, merge, and compose commits, when [Agent tools](#agent-tools) turns them on.

Every workspace tool runs without the agent's own permission prompt, in both Chat and Terminal. Instead, an action that needs your approval, such as deleting a worktree or changing another task, waits for you on an approval card. See [Approvals](#approvals), and [Tasks and Resources](/kepler/tasks-and-resources) for the full list of tools.

## Agent tools

Use **Agent tools** to let your agents call Kepler's own tools for rebasing, merging, and cleaning up commits:

| Setting | What it does | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **AI Sync** | *Lets agents rebase or merge your branch and resolve conflicts for you. Every change can be undone.* | Off |
| **AI Compose** | *Lets agents turn messy changes into clean, focused commits. Every change can be undone.* | Off |

**AI Sync** and **AI Compose** add their tools to the workspace MCP server. You need a paid GitKraken subscription to turn either one on. On the Community plan, when you are signed out, or with no organization, a setting that is off shows a lock in place of its checkbox: *Not available on the Community plan. Upgrade to unlock.* A setting that is already on keeps its checkbox, so you can still turn it off.

When you turn either setting on, Kepler confirms that *New agent sessions will pick up this change.* Sessions already running keep the tools they started with.

## Approvals

Some actions your agents take wait for your approval. Use **Approvals** to manage the rules that approve those actions for you. An action that no rule covers still asks.

When an agent uses Kepler's workspace tools to do something that needs your approval, Kepler pins an approval card above that session's message box. Examples include deleting a worktree, sending a prompt to another session, or rewriting a branch. The card's **Approve** menu offers **Always approve** for that kind of action. Kepler does not offer it for actions that can lose work, or for a setting change that Ask Kepler asks to make. See [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions).

**Always approved** lists each rule you create this way. A rule's row says when and where you added it, *Added {date} from {session} on {task}.*, and how often it has run, *Used {count} times, last {when}.* or *Not used yet.* **Remove** deletes the rule, so that kind of action asks again. With no rules, the section reads *No rules yet. When an agent asks, choose Always approve on its request to stop being asked about actions like it.*

## Usage limits

These settings control how Kepler handles your agent plans' usage limits:

| Setting | What it controls | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **Check plan usage with each agent's provider** | *Kepler asks each agent's provider for your plan usage, per-model limits and extra usage, using the agent's own sign-in. The sign-in goes nowhere else and is never changed. When off, Kepler shows only what agents report, and a message queued at a usage limit is sent automatically only if the agent says when the limit resets.* | On |
| **Resume after the usage limit resets** | When your account usage limit cuts off a turn and nothing is queued, Kepler queues a "continue" message and sends it shortly after the limit resets | Off |

***

---

---
# Task Settings
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/settings-tasks/
product: Kepler
feature: Settings
content_type: reference
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-10

Use **Settings → Tasks** to choose how new tasks start and how a task's page looks. A task is one piece of work: its prompt, the agent sessions working on it, and the worktree or folder they work in.

## New tasks

**New tasks** sets what Kepler preselects for every new task: the agent, where the task makes changes, how branches and folders are named, and whether Kepler names the task for you. These values belong to the environment you are working on, so in a remote window they are the remote machine's.

### Default agent

**Default agent** picks the agent, account, model, mode, and thinking effort that Kepler preselects for a new task. Its description reads *Used when new sessions start with the default agent, when Kepler has no earlier pick to go on, and whenever you choose Use default agent in the launcher.* The following table lists its controls:

| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| **New tasks use** | Chooses the agent, and the account when that agent supports more than one |
| Options | Model, mode, and the agent's own configuration options. Available once an agent is picked |
| **Clear default** | Removes the saved default. Appears only once one is set |

No default agent is set out of the box. If no agent is installed, Kepler hides the control. If you later uninstall the agent you saved, the row warns you: *Your default agent, {name}, is no longer installed. Pick another.*

An [Action](/kepler/actions) inherits this configuration unless it names an agent of its own.

### New sessions start with

Under **Default agent**, the following setting decides which agent the **New task** composer, the Dashboard's composer, and a new draft session preselect:

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Last used agent** | *The agent, model and mode you last picked.* The default |
| **Default agent** | *Always the default agent above.* |

With **Last used agent**, a task that an agent created and that has no session yet starts with the agent that created it. Kepler does not remember an Action's own agent as your last pick. If you choose **Default agent** with no default set, Kepler points you to the **Default agent** picker. Neither setting applies to Ask Kepler, which keeps its own last pick and its own default in [Settings → Agents](/kepler/settings-agents).

### Where new tasks make changes

The following setting chooses what a repository starts on when you attach it to a new task:

| Setting | What it controls | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **Where new tasks make changes** | What a newly attached repository starts on, in the **New task** composer | Isolated worktree |

The setting has these options:

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Isolated worktree** | *Own folder, agents run side by side.* Forks a new branch into its own worktree |
| **New branch** | *Switches your repo to a new branch.* Forks a new branch directly in the repository's own checkout, with no worktree |
| **Current branch** | *Works on whatever is checked out.* Runs on the repository's own checkout, on whichever branch it currently has, with no new branch created |

This setting is only the default. For a single task, the repository chip's own **Base branch** and **Isolated worktree** controls override it. See [Create a task](/kepler/create-task#configuring-a-repository).

**Commits made on the current branch land on whichever branch is checked out at the time.** This applies to both **New branch** and **Current branch**, because both run in the repository's own checkout instead of an isolated one. If another task is already working in that checkout, Kepler says so and offers to switch that repository to an isolated worktree instead.

**Branch prefix** and **Worktrees folder** appear under **Where new tasks make changes**, because they apply only when Kepler creates a branch or a worktree.

### Branch prefix

The following setting starts the name of every branch Kepler creates:

| Setting | What it controls | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **Branch prefix** | *Starts the name of every branch Kepler creates. A repo can set its own in its settings.* | `kepler/` |

The prefix applies to **automatic** names only. Kepler uses a branch name you type exactly as you typed it, so a repository with an enforced `feat/` or `fix/` push rule still works. If you type a prefix without a trailing separator, Kepler adds a `/`, so typing `team` stores `team/`. A prefix that already ends in a separator, such as `ea-`, stays exactly as you typed it. The prefix saves when you press **Enter** or **Escape**, or leave the field, and the field shows its save status.

To override the prefix for one repository, use its [Edit repo](/kepler/settings-repositories#edit-a-repository) page under **Settings → Repositories**. If a repository already has a branch named exactly like the prefix, Kepler names the branch and points you to that page: *Can't be used in {repo}: it has a branch named {branch}. Set a different prefix for that repository under Repositories.*

### Folder locations

Kepler uses 3 folder settings to decide where to put things. The first 2 are under **Tasks → New tasks**, and the third is on the **Repositories** page:

| Setting | Where it is | What it controls | Default |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Worktrees folder** | Tasks → New tasks | *Where Kepler creates the worktree for each new task.* | `~/kepler/worktrees` |
| **Tasks folder** | Tasks → New tasks | *Each task gets a folder here for its attachments and files.* | `~/kepler/tasks` |
| **Repositories folder** | [Repositories](/kepler/settings-repositories#repositories-folder) | Where Kepler clones repositories, and where it looks for repositories to add | `~/kepler/repositories` |

All 3 are unset out of the box. Until you set one, Kepler uses the default under your home folder without saving it, so the setting stays unset.

Type a path directly, or click **Choose a folder** beside the field to browse. An edit saves when you leave the field, so there is no **Save** button. The field shows its save status.

The fields also warn you about paths that do not work the way you might expect:

- If a **Worktrees folder** has text before `<REPOSITORY_PATH>`, Kepler adds each repository's full path after that text. The field tells you so, *Each repo's full path is added after this folder.*, and shows where an example repository would go. It also suggests 2 templates: one for worktrees next to each repository, and one for a subfolder per repository. On Windows, such a path is invalid, so Kepler does not save it: *Not saved: adding each repo's full path after this folder creates an invalid path.*
- If the **Repositories folder** does not exist yet, the field reads *This folder doesn't exist yet. Kepler creates it when you clone.*

### The Variables menu

A folder field that can contain a dynamic variable has a **Variables** menu beside it. The menu shows each variable as a named tag, such as **REPOSITORY PATH**, beside its raw token. When you pick a variable, Kepler inserts it at the cursor. Kepler fills in the variable when it creates the folder, so one pattern works for every repository. Each field offers only the variables it can fill in:

| Field | Variables offered |
|---|---|
| **Worktrees folder** | `<REPOSITORY_PATH>` (*Main repo folder*), `<REPOSITORY_NAME>` (*Repo name*) |
| **Repositories folder** | `<REPOSITORY_NAME>` |
| **Tasks folder** | None |

For example, `<REPOSITORY_PATH>/.worktrees/<REPOSITORY_NAME>` nests each worktree inside the repository it belongs to. Kepler collapses any `..` segments you write.

**Tasks folder** takes no variables. A task folder has no repository behind it, so nothing would ever fill one in. Kepler does not save such a value: *Dynamic variables cannot be used here. A task folder has no repository behind it, so nothing would ever fill one in. This value was not saved.*

Per-repository commands have a **Variables** menu of their own, with 2 more variables. See [Per-repository commands](/kepler/settings-repositories#per-repository-commands).

### Automatically name new tasks

The following setting names new tasks for you:

| Setting | What it controls | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **Automatically name new tasks** | *Names a new task with AI from its prompt and attached resources. A task created from a single issue or PR keeps that item's name.* | On |

You need a paid GitKraken subscription to turn this setting on. On the Community plan, when you are signed out, or with no organization, a lock replaces the checkbox only while the setting is off. Because the setting starts on, you see a ticked checkbox, and you can always turn it off. A change takes effect on the next task you create.

## Task page

**Task page** sets how a task's page looks in this window. Kepler saves these settings on this machine:

| Setting | What it controls | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **Show tabs on the task page** | Keeps sessions, worktrees, and resources open as tabs you can pin, drag between groups, and arrange side by side. With it off, each column of a task shows one thing at a time, and you switch between them from the list on the left | Off |
| **Preview tabs** | *A single click opens a preview that the next click replaces. Double-click, or edit, to keep it open.* | On |

**Preview tabs** works only with **Show tabs on the task page** turned on. Sessions always open as permanent tabs. See [The task view](/kepler/task-view).

***

---

---
# Repository Settings
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/settings-repositories/
product: Kepler
feature: Settings
content_type: reference
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-10

Use **Settings → Repositories** to choose where Kepler clones repositories, add and edit the repositories and folders Kepler tracks, update and clean up worktrees and branches, and group repositories into projects.

## Repositories folder

The following setting tells Kepler where to clone repositories:

| Setting | What it controls | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **Repositories folder** | *Kepler adds the repos it finds in this folder. It only looks when you change the folder or scan, so a repo you remove won't come back.* | `~/kepler/repositories` |

To add every repository already in that folder, click **Scan for repositories** beside the field. A notification reports **Added {count} repositories.** or **No new repositories found.** Kepler scans only when you change the setting or click the button, never on startup, so a repository you removed stays removed.

After a scan that added repositories, **Undo** removes them again. Undo keeps any repository you have started using or changed since the scan, and names it: *Kept {names}. You've used or changed them since the scan.* If nothing before a variable in the setting is a full folder path, the scan has nowhere to look and says so: *There is no folder to scan: nothing before the dynamic variable in this setting is a full folder path. Point it at one first.*

If the folder does not exist yet, the field says that Kepler creates it when you clone. The field takes the `<REPOSITORY_NAME>` variable. See [The Variables menu](/kepler/settings-tasks#the-variables-menu).

## Your repos and folders

**Your repos and folders** lists every repository Kepler tracks and every folder you have attached to a task. Each row shows its name, its path on disk, and how many commands it has: **No commands**, **1 command**, or a count. The section has these controls:

| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Filter repos and folders** | Narrows the list by name |
| A row | Click it to open the repository's **Edit repo** page, or the folder's page |
| **Add repo** | Opens the **Add repo** page. See below |
| **Add folder…** | Adds a plain folder |
| Trash icon | Stops tracking the repository or folder. Kepler leaves the folder on disk as it is |

With nothing tracked, the section reads *Add a repository or folder to manage it here.*

Removing a repository deletes its sessions, terminals, and configured commands, and ends any live agent and terminal sessions tied to it. Kepler asks you to confirm first.

### Add a repository

To add a repository, click **Add repo**. On the sub-page that opens, give a source. Kepler inspects it and shows what it found as a card you can edit before you add it:

| Field | What it takes |
|---|---|
| **Folder or URL** | *Paste a URL to clone it, or pick a folder that already holds a repo.* You can also drop a folder onto the page, or **Create a new repo instead** |
| The card | The resolved repository (**{name} on {provider}**, its path, its branch count), plus the name, description, and branch prefix you can edit |

Before you add it, Kepler tells you what the source is. For example, it reads **A new folder named {name} will be created here.**, *This folder already holds a clone of that repo. It will be added as is.*, or **This repo is already in Kepler.** A path that is not a Git repository reads **That folder isn't a Git repo.**

While a clone runs, the page reads *Cloning {name} into {folder}* and *You can leave this page. Kepler tells you when the clone finishes.* Leaving does not stop the clone. If it fails later, a notification names the repository: *Unable to clone {name}: {reason}*.

### Edit a repository

Click a repository's row to open its **Edit repo** page. The page shows the repository's path, its remote, and its branches, and has these parts:

| Part | What it holds |
|---|---|
| **Name** | The name Kepler shows wherever it names this repository. Leave it empty to use the folder name, which is the field's placeholder |
| **Aliases** | *Short names for this repo when talking to agents, separated by commas.* An agent can use an alias wherever Kepler's workspace tools take a repository, and finds the repository by alias when it lists your repositories |
| **Description** | Free text. Its placeholder reads *What this repo is for. Agents working in it read this.* |
| **Branch prefix** | Overrides the prefix from **Settings → Tasks** for this repository only. See below |
| **Commands** | Shell commands for this repository. See [Per-repository commands](#per-repository-commands) |
| **MCP servers** | *Extra tools your agents get in this repo, on top of their own lists. Changes here apply right away.* See [MCP Servers](/kepler/mcp-servers) |

**Name**, **Aliases**, and **Description** are optional, and Kepler stores text that is only spaces as empty. The page has no **Save** button: each field saves on its own and shows its save status. Some fields have more rules:

- A repository you name keeps that name exactly, and Kepler no longer adds a suffix to tell it apart from folders with the same name.
- An alias cannot contain a colon, or repeat another repository's alias or name.
- Kepler adds the description to the repository's line in the resource list it gives a session, so a full sentence helps more than a single label.

#### Branch prefix, per repository

The **Branch prefix** control has 3 options:

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Default ({value})** | Uses the prefix from **Settings → Tasks** |
| **None** | Creates task branches with no prefix |
| **Custom** | A prefix for this repository only |

**New task branches will look like** shows an example, so you can see what you are choosing before a branch exists.

**Default** and **None** save as soon as you pick them. **Custom** saves its text when you press **Enter** or **Escape**, or leave the field. If the repository already has a local branch named like the prefix, Kepler does not save the prefix: *Can't create {prefix} branches here: this repo already has a branch named {branch}. Rename that branch or choose another prefix.*

### Per-repository commands

Use commands to run your dev server, tests, or build from a task's worktree in one click. A command can also run when Kepler creates a new worktree, for example to install dependencies. Commands are shell commands for one repository.

To add a command, click **Add command** in the **Commands** section of the Edit repo page. With no commands, the section reads *No commands yet.* and suggests examples. Each command row has 3 fields:

| Field | What it does |
|---|---|
| Name | A label, for example *Install deps*. You pick the command by this name from the **Run** menu |
| Command | The shell command, for example `pnpm install`. Its **Variables** menu inserts any of the variables below |
| **Run on worktree creation** | Runs the command automatically when Kepler creates a worktree for this repository, and shows a **Runs on creation** chip on the row. Off by default, so the command runs only when you start it |

Each command saves on its own. An open row has **Cancel** and a primary button: **Add command** for a new row, or **Save** for a stored one. To save the row from the keyboard, press **Enter** in the name field, or **⌘ Enter** (**Ctrl + Enter** on Windows and Linux).

Commands accept 4 variables, which Kepler fills in when the command runs:

| Variable | Resolves to |
|---|---|
| `<REPOSITORY_PATH>` | Main repo folder |
| `<REPOSITORY_NAME>` | Repo name |
| `<SOURCE_PATH>` | Where files come from (the main repo, or the source worktree when forking) |
| `<WORKTREE_PATH>` | The new worktree folder |

To reorder commands, drag a row by its handle, or move it from the keyboard with **Alt + ↑** and **Alt + ↓**. A new order saves at once. The order sets the order of the **Run** menu, and the order in which commands set to run on worktree creation run.

You cannot save a row that is missing its name or its command. Kepler opens the row on the missing field, with *Add a name to show in the Run menu.* or *Add the command to run.* **Cancel** discards a row you opened by accident. A closed row that is not saved yet shows a **Not saved** chip. **Remove command** deletes a saved command at once, and a *Deleted command {name}* notification offers **Undo**.

Commands set to run on worktree creation run one at a time, in list order. If one fails, Kepler skips the rest and reports them as skipped. Each command runs in the new worktree's folder through your login shell, so you do not need to `cd` into it, and tools set up in your shell profile, such as `nvm`, are available. Each command has a 10-minute timeout.

A failed command does not undo the worktree. The worktree exists but may not be usable. To fix it:

1. Read the command output in the task.
2. Correct the command here.
3. Run it again from the **Run** menu.

To run a command from the task view, right-click a worktree row in the task's context panel and use **Run command here**. It lists that repository's commands and runs the one you pick in that worktree, with its terminal opening in place. For a repository with no commands yet, the menu reads **No commands yet** and offers **Create command…**. That item opens the Edit repo page, and returns you to the task when you leave the page. A running command shows on the run button and its menus, where you can stop it.

## Worktrees and branches

To update, clean up, or delete worktrees and local branches across your repositories, click **Manage worktrees and branches** on the Repositories page. The **Worktrees and branches** sub-page opens.

On the sub-page, you can see which worktrees and local branches are stale, update the ones that can be brought up to date, and delete what is done. The sub-page checks your repositories as soon as it opens, and deletes nothing until you ask. It lists every worktree, and every local branch that no worktree holds, grouped by repository. A summary such as *{worktrees} and {branches} in {repos}.* says how many look safe to delete. A branch with no worktree reads **Not checked out** where a worktree shows its path. The base branch has a **Base** badge, and Kepler never deletes it.

The sub-page has these controls:

| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Search branch, path or repo** | Narrows the list. Every word you type must match the branch, the path, or the repository name |
| **Show worktrees and branches** | Filters by status: **Safe to delete ({count})**, **Needs update ({count})**, **Conflicts ({count})**, **Stale ({count})**, or **All ({count})**. A count reads *checking…* until Kepler has compared each branch with its base |
| **Show worktrees, branches or both** | **All**, **Worktrees only**, or **Branches only** |
| **Stale after** *n* **days** | How many days without activity before a worktree or branch counts as stale. Defaults to 14 |
| **Re-check** | Fetches every repository's remotes, then inspects the list again. A repository whose fetch failed says so beside its name: *Unable to fetch: {reason}; numbers may be stale* |
| **Select all safe to delete** / **Select all that need an update** / **Select all with conflicts** / **Select all stale** / **Select all** | Selects the rows in the current view |
| Selection bar | Reads *{count} selected*, or *{count} selected · {hidden} hidden by filters*, with **Clear**, **Create task**, **Update**, and **Delete**. **Update** and **Delete** act only on the selected rows you can see |

**Create task** opens the **New task** composer with the selected worktrees and branches already added: each worktree as it is, and each branch without a worktree as a branch to work on. Kepler creates nothing until you start or prepare the task. See [Create a task](/kepler/create-task).

Each row shows the following:

- Where it stands with its upstream: commits to push (↑) and pull (↓), **No upstream**, or **Upstream gone**.
- How it compares with its base, as a badge: **{count} behind {base}**, **Conflicts with {base}**, or **Up to date with {base}**, plus how many files are uncommitted.
- How long since it was last touched, and why it may be finished, such as being merged into its base.
- The tasks using it, an **External** count for sessions started outside Kepler, and its pull request. A branch row shows the tasks, sessions, and pull requests tied to that branch.

With a Jira or Jira Server account connected, a row whose branch name references a Jira issue shows a chip for that issue under the branch name. To open the issue in your browser, click the chip. Its tooltip shows the issue's URL. When Kepler cannot match every reference, the row reads **Issue reference matching limit reached**. See [Issue Tracker Integrations](/kepler/issue-tracker-integrations).

A row counts as one or more of the following:

- **Safe to delete**: *Its work has landed: merged into the base or its pull request merged (a branch whose upstream is gone and whose pull request was closed counts too), and nothing is uncommitted, unpushed or in use.*
- **Needs update**: behind the base branch with no known conflict, so an update can bring it up to date.
- **Conflicts**: behind the base branch, and merging the base in would conflict, so you have to update it by hand.
- **Stale**: no activity for longer than the stale threshold, but nothing proves the work landed. It may still hold uncommitted or unpushed work, so deleting it can lose something.

**Needs update** and **Conflicts** leave out rows that are safe to delete. Activity includes what Kepler recorded on the branch, not only changes in the worktree.

### Delete worktrees and branches

Select rows, then click **Delete**. The confirmation, **Delete {count} items?**, says what is lost:

- For worktrees: *The directories are removed from disk. Anything listed below is lost with them.* **Also delete the branches** deletes each worktree's branch too.
- For local branches: *The local branches are deleted. Commits that exist only on them are lost.* When every branch's work has landed, it reads *Their work is already in the base branch, so nothing is lost.* instead. The dialog marks each branch that is not merged as **not merged**. **Force delete branches that are not merged** deletes those too, and **Also delete the branches on the remote** deletes the remote branches.

Kepler keeps any branch it cannot delete safely and says why, for example *Checked out in {path}. Remove that worktree first.* or *Its work is not in the base branch, so it was kept.*

Kepler never deletes a repository's main checkout. It keeps any worktree that still has uncommitted or unpushed work, other tasks, running agent sessions, or a lock from another tool, and says why for each one. If Kepler itself locked a worktree, for a task this install knows or a task since deleted, Kepler clears the lock and deletes the worktree. Where forcing can help, the result offers **Force delete**, which discards the listed work and ends the agent sessions running there.

### Update worktrees

To bring several worktrees and local branches up to date with their base branch at once:

1. On the Worktrees and branches sub-page, select the worktrees and branches.
2. Click **Update**. The **Update worktrees** dialog opens: *Each branch is brought up to date with its base. Nothing changes until Update is pressed.*
3. Review the plan. Each row reads **Will update** with how many commits it's behind, **Up to date**, or **Skipped** with the reason, such as *an agent is working in it*, *uncommitted changes*, *checked out in a worktree*, *would conflict*, or *a sync result is waiting for review*.
4. Under **How to update**, choose **Rebase** or **Merge**.
5. To push each updated branch too, tick **Push after update**. Each row that will update then reads **Will push**, or **No upstream, update only** for a branch with no upstream.
6. Click **Update**.

Kepler updates a local branch that has no worktree in place, from the repository's main checkout, without checking it out. It skips such a branch when a worktree holds it, or when the main checkout has uncommitted changes. If Kepler prepared an update but could not apply it automatically, Kepler keeps it for you to review instead of discarding it.

While the update runs, each row shows its status: **Waiting**, **Updating…**, **Updated**, **Up to date**, **Skipped**, **Conflict**, or **Failed**. When it finishes, you can undo one row with **Roll back**, or every row with **Roll back all**. If you did not push during the update, **Push** and **Push all** push the updated branches that have an upstream. Kepler does not push a branch that moved since the update. The finished report stays in every window until you click **Dismiss**.

## Projects

Use **Projects** to group repositories that belong together under one name, such as a frontend and a backend you change together. A **Project**'s repositories act as a unit. The section has these controls:

| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| A row | Shows the project's name and its repository count. Click it to open the project's page |
| **New project** | Opens a page where you name a project and pick its repositories. **Add from folder** adds a repository without leaving the page |

With no projects, the section reads *No projects yet.*

A new project shows **Create** and **Cancel**. **Create** does not accept a blank name: *Give the project a name.* Once the project exists, its page has no **Save** button. Its name saves as you edit it, and each repository you tick or untick saves at once. A folder's page saves its name and description the same way.

To delete a project, click **Delete project** on its page. Its repositories stay in your repository list.

***

---

---
# Integration Settings
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/settings-integrations/
product: Kepler
feature: Settings
content_type: reference
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-10

Use **Settings → Integrations** to connect the issue trackers and Git hosts you start tasks from, and to follow agent sessions you run in your own terminal.

## Issues and pull requests

Connect your issue and pull request providers to see their issues and pull requests in the **New task** composer and in [the Kepler interface](/kepler/kepler-interface). Kepler lists every supported provider, connected or not, in this order:

| Provider |
|---|
| Azure DevOps |
| Azure DevOps Server |
| Bitbucket |
| Bitbucket Data Center |
| GitHub |
| GitHub Enterprise |
| GitLab |
| GitLab Self-Hosted |
| Jira |
| Jira Server / Data Center |
| Linear |
| Trello |

Each provider row shows these controls and states:

| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Connect** | Starts the connection flow for a provider you have not connected |
| **Connected** | Shown on a working connection |
| **Reconnect** | Refreshes an expired token. A **Sign-in expired** badge and the hint *Sign-in has expired. Click Reconnect to refresh this provider's token.* mark the rows that need it |
| **Cannot connect to server** | The provider's server did not answer. The integration stays connected and this state clears by itself once the server responds, so you do not need to reconnect |
| **Unexpected response** | The provider answered with data Kepler could not read, so some of its items may be missing. The integration stays connected, and reconnecting does not fix this state |
| **Disconnect** | Disconnects the provider from GitKraken everywhere: every GitKraken product and service that uses this connection loses access too. Other accounts for that provider stay connected, and you can reconnect at any time |
| **Refresh** | Checks every provider's connection status again. It is in the section header |

If a row shows **Cannot connect to server**, check that the server is reachable from your network or VPN. If **Unexpected response** stays, check for a proxy or gateway between Kepler and the provider.

Providers connect through your GitKraken account, so the section asks you to sign in before it shows anything to manage.

A self-hosted provider, such as GitHub Enterprise, Azure DevOps Server, Bitbucket Data Center, or Jira Server / Data Center, connects with a personal access token. **Connect** or **Reconnect** opens **Connect {name}**, with **Server URL** and **Personal access token**. **Save connection** checks the token against your server from this machine, saves the connection here, and syncs it to your GitKraken account. Until the sync finishes, the row shows **Cloud sync pending**. See [Pull Request Integrations](/kepler/pull-request-integrations) and [Issue Tracker Integrations](/kepler/issue-tracker-integrations).

To hide organizations, repositories, or tracker projects you do not want in Kepler, use **Choose what's visible…**. Every connected provider except Trello has it, on a line that reads **Everything visible** or **{count} hidden**. In **Choose what {name} brings in**, untick the items to hide. *Hidden items are left out of the dashboard, the launcher and pickers. Tasks and branches already linked to them keep resolving.* Kepler saves the choice on your GitKraken account. See [Issue Tracker Integrations](/kepler/issue-tracker-integrations).

When a provider has more than 1 account, an **Accounts** block lists them. **Set as primary** chooses which account Kepler acts as, and **Read from this account** chooses which account Kepler reads issues and pull requests from. These can be different accounts.

When an organization refuses a working connection, because it blocks third-party OAuth apps or has not approved GitKraken, the row names the organization and says that its items are not shown. The row links to a fix, such as **Request access on GitHub**.

Under the list, the line *Agents can use these through the GitKraken MCP server.* links to [MCP servers](/kepler/settings-agents#mcp-servers).

For per-provider setup, see [Issue Tracker Integrations](/kepler/issue-tracker-integrations) and [Pull Request Integrations](/kepler/pull-request-integrations).

## Your terminal

The following setting lets you follow agent sessions you start outside Kepler:

| Setting | What it controls | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **Show sessions started outside Kepler** | *Lists sessions you start in your own terminal, so you can follow and continue them here.* | On |

To do this, Kepler installs GitKraken hooks. The switch covers every agent that reports through hooks, and its help text names those agents. See [Agent Sessions](/kepler/agent-sessions#sessions-started-outside-kepler).

If Kepler stops receiving hook events from a running agent session, every window shows *Agent sessions aren't reporting to Kepler*, with a **Repair** button. **Repair** installs the reporting configuration again. A running CLI does not reload its hooks, so restart any session that still does not report. A window that only views another computer's sessions shows the warning without **Repair**, and tells you to repair reporting from the computer running those sessions.

***

---

---
# Action Settings
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/settings-actions/
product: Kepler
feature: Settings
content_type: reference
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-10

Use **Settings → Actions** to save the prompts you use often and run them on a task, issue, or pull request without typing them again. An **Action** is an editable named prompt. The page has these sections:

| Section | What it holds |
|---|---|
| **Preferred Actions** | Which Action runs when you press the Action button on a task, issue, or pull request: one picker each for **Tasks**, **Issues**, **Pull requests I authored**, and **Pull requests from others**. Any picker can be **None** |
| **All Actions** | The built-in Actions under **Built in**, and yours under **Custom**. Click a row to edit it, use **Restore default** on a row you have edited, or use **Delete** on a custom row |

To create an Action, click **New Action** in the **All Actions** section header. **Restore all defaults**, beside it, discards every edit. An Action you create or edit opens as a sub-page.

Kepler has 4 built-in Actions, and each one is the default preferred Action for one kind of item:

- **Tasks** default to **Implement**.
- **Issues** default to **Plan**.
- Pull requests you authored default to **Address Feedback**.
- Pull requests from others default to **Review**.

For what the built-in Actions ask an agent to do, how the editor's **Title**, **Prompt**, **Applies to**, and **Agent** fields behave, and how an Action picks the agent it runs on, see [Actions](/kepler/actions).

***

---

---
# App Settings
URL: https://help.gitkraken.com/kepler/settings-app/
product: Kepler
feature: Settings
content_type: reference
audience: developer
plan_required: all
status: GA
last_verified: 2026-10

Use these Settings pages to change how Kepler itself looks and behaves:

- [General](#general): language, windows, the default editor, and keeping agents running
- [Notifications](#notifications): which agent events notify you, on the desktop and in Kepler
- [Appearance](#appearance): light or dark appearance and themes, the chat, the terminal font, code font size, and diff layout
- [Voice input](#voice-input): on-device speech-to-text, its transcription engine, and learned words
- [Keyboard shortcuts](#keyboard-shortcuts): Kepler's keyboard shortcuts

***

## General

Use **General** to choose Kepler's language, how its windows open, which editor opens your files, and whether agents keep running when your machine would sleep or Kepler restarts.

### Language

**Language** has 1 setting:

| Setting | What it controls | Default | Options |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Language** | The display language for Kepler's interface | English | English, Español |

The language also applies to native dialogs, not only to the in-app interface.

### Windows

These settings set how windows work on this machine:

| Setting | What it controls | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **Restore windows on launch** | *Reopens the windows you had open, with their size, page and connection. Turn off to start with one window.* | On |
| **Always use the custom folder picker** | Local windows open your system's folder dialog, and windows connected to another machine use Kepler's own folder picker, which can browse that machine. Turn this on to use Kepler's picker in every window | Off |

Kepler reads **Restore windows on launch** only when it starts, so a change takes effect the next time you start Kepler.

### Default editor

**Default editor** has 1 setting:

| Setting | What it controls | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **Open files and folders in** | The app that **Open in** and **⌘ ⇧**-click (**Ctrl + Shift**-click on Windows and Linux) on a file link use. The options are **Last used app**, each editor Kepler finds on this machine, and your system's default app | Last used app |

With your system's default app, files open without line numbers, folders open in Finder, Explorer, or your file manager, and programs open in your last used editor. If Kepler cannot open any editor from the window you are in, the setting reads *No editors can be opened from this window*.

### Keep agents running

These settings keep agent work running when the machine would otherwise stop it. They apply to the machine the agents run on, so in a window connected to a remote machine, they apply to that machine:

| Setting | What it controls | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **Keep this machine awake while agents work** | Blocks sleep and standby while an agent session is starting, running, or waiting for your input. It also blocks sleep while Remote Access is on, because sleeping would drop the connection, but not while Remote Access is waiting to reconnect | On |
| **Keep agents and terminals running across restarts and updates** | *Agent sessions and terminals stay alive while Kepler restarts or updates, and reconnect afterwards. Experimental.* | On |

To keep the machine awake, Kepler uses the platform's own method: `caffeinate` on macOS, an execution-state assertion on Windows, and `systemd-inhibit` on Linux. The screen can still turn off. If Kepler cannot keep the machine awake, the setting says so under the switch, for example *Can't stay awake: there is no sleep-blocking mechanism available on this platform.* On Linux, the setting can say that the system's polkit policy refuses the request, and give a rule an administrator can install.

The setting counts Claude Code sessions detected outside Kepler as well as Kepler's own sessions. Kepler lets the machine sleep again as soon as the last of those sessions settles.

**Keep agents and terminals running across restarts and updates** applies from the next session you start. With it on, a ready update's popover says *Running agents and open terminals keep going through the restart.* On a build that does not include the runtime this setting needs, the switch shows off, is disabled, and says so: *This build can't keep agents running across restarts.*

***

## Notifications

Use **Notifications** to choose which agent events Kepler tells you about, and where. **Desktop** notifications show while Kepler is in the background, and **In Kepler** alerts show while you are using it. Sessions started outside Kepler notify you only once they are on a task. Kepler saves these settings on this machine.

### What to notify you about

**What to notify you about** is a grid. Each row is an event, and each column is a place Kepler can notify you: **Desktop** or **In Kepler**. The following table lists the events and their defaults in the desktop app:

| Event | When it fires | Desktop | In Kepler |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Replies** | *An agent finished replying and it's your turn.* | Off | Off |
| **Questions** | *An agent asks you something and waits for your answer.* | On | On |
| **Permission requests** | *An agent wants permission to do something.* | On | On |
| **Approval requests** | *An agent asks to do something in Kepler only you can approve, like deleting a worktree or rewriting a branch.* See [Approvals](/kepler/settings-agents#approvals) | On | On |
| **Errors** | *A session stops because something went wrong.* | On | On |

In a browser connected to Kepler, every **Desktop** box starts off. **Replies** stays off on the desktop unless you turned on system notifications in an earlier version of Kepler. Until you set **Approval requests** yourself, it follows **Permission requests**. When you turn on the first **Desktop** box, Kepler sends a sample notification so your OS asks for permission.

After your first session starts, the desktop app sends 1 notification to say *Notifications are on*: *Kepler will notify you here when an agent needs you. Change this in Settings › Notifications.* Click the notification to open **Settings → Notifications**. If every **Desktop** box is off, Kepler skips this notification.

These settings appear under the grid:

| Setting | What it controls | Default |
|---|---|---|
| **Play a sound with desktop notifications** | Whether a desktop notification makes the OS notification sound | On |
| **Notify even for the task you're looking at** | *Otherwise Kepler stays quiet about the task open in the window you're using.* | Off |

To silence desktop notifications from one remote machine only, use **Mute notifications from {host}** on that machine in [Remote environments](/kepler/settings-environment#remote-environments).

***

## Appearance

Use **Appearance** to choose light or dark and a theme, and to set up the chat, the terminal, code text, and diffs. Kepler saves these settings on this machine.

### Theme

The **Theme** section has 2 parts: **Appearance**, which picks whether Kepler looks light or dark, and **Theme**, which picks the colors for each. Themes color the whole app, including code views, diffs, syntax, chat code blocks, and terminals.

**Appearance** has 3 options:

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| **System** | *Follows your system.* Kepler uses your dark theme when your OS is dark and your light theme when it's light, and switches when the OS does. **The default** |
| **Light** | *Always uses a light theme* |
| **Dark** | *Always uses a dark theme* |

Under **Theme**, each theme is a tile. The **Kepler** group holds the built-in themes:

- **Kepler**, which has a dark and a light version. It's the theme a fresh install uses for both.
- **Midnight**, a near-black theme that has only a dark version.

How you pick a tile depends on **Appearance**:

- On **System**, each tile has a moon and a sun. Click the moon to *Use {name} when your system is dark*, or the sun to *Use {name} when your system is light*. Click the tile itself to *Use {name} for both dark and light*.
- On **Light** or **Dark**, click a tile to use it for that appearance.

The tile in use reads **In use now**. If you used **Midnight** in an earlier version of Kepler, Kepler switches **Appearance** to **Dark** and keeps **Midnight** as your dark theme.

Terminals follow the theme too. When a terminal program asks, such as an agent's own command-line app, Kepler tells it the terminal's background color as it starts, so the program can draw colors that suit your theme. If a running program asks to follow theme changes, Kepler redraws it when you switch themes.

#### Your themes

**Your themes** lists the themes you have added, with 2 more tiles, **Browse gallery** and **Create a theme**. **Open themes folder**, beside the heading, opens the folder that holds your themes, `~/.kepler/themes`.

A theme file follows these rules:

- It is a `.json` or `.jsonc` file, so comments are allowed.
- A single file can hold a family of up to 8 themes, such as a dark and a light version.
- Each theme has an id and a name, and `extends` one of Kepler's base themes: `midnight`, `dark`, or `light`. The theme then overrides that base's colors, and can add code colors and a `terminal` block.
- The `terminal` block sets the terminal's background, foreground, cursor, selection, and 16 ANSI colors.

Kepler reads up to 64 theme files, and reloads a file each time you save it.

If Kepler cannot fully read a theme's file, its tile shows **Has problems** or **Has warnings**. To see what is wrong, click the badge. A file that is not valid JSON shows *Line {line}, column {column}: {message}*. A problem with a theme's values names the setting it is in, such as *themes.1.extends*.

A file with warnings still works. Kepler leaves out a theme that has errors, and still loads the other themes in its file. To fix a file, use one of these options below the list of problems:

- **Create a task to fix it** gives the file to an agent.
- In the desktop app, **Open file** opens the file in your editor, at the error's line when there is one. *Changes apply when you save.*

A tile's **More actions for {name}** menu has **Show in folder** and **Move to Trash** (**Move to Recycle Bin** on Windows).

#### Theme gallery

**Browse gallery** opens the **Theme gallery**: *Themes from the community, each checked for contrast. Try one on Kepler before you install it.* The gallery needs an internet connection. It has the following controls:

- **Search themes**, which matches a theme's name, author, tags, or description.
- **Show**, which filters to **All**, **Dark**, or **Light** themes.
- **Sort:**, with **Featured**, **Newest**, or **Name**.

Click a theme to see its details card, drawn in the theme's own colors. The card shows its author, its dark and light variants, **Version**, **License**, and **Updated**, and any contrast warnings in your version of Kepler. Then choose one of the following:

- **Install** adds the theme to **Your themes** without changing the theme on screen. The button then reads **Use**, or **Use for dark and light** for a theme with both.
- **Try it** closes the gallery and paints the whole window in the theme, so you can open a diff or a terminal to judge it. A bar at the bottom reads **Trying {name}**, with **Use {name}** and **Done**, which returns you to the gallery.

If a theme you already have uses the same id, Kepler asks before it replaces that file, and moves the old file to the Trash. A gallery theme you installed and have not edited offers **Update to {version}** on its tile when a newer version is published. The gallery's themes come from `gitkraken/kepler-themes` on GitHub, where you can also publish your own.

#### Create a theme

**Create a theme** opens the new task launcher with a prompt already written for an agent, ending in *The theme I want:* for you to describe it. The agent reads and saves themes through Kepler's `theme_get` and `theme_save` tools, so it does not need the themes folder attached. Before `theme_save` saves a theme, it checks the file's format and that its colors reach the minimum contrast Kepler requires, and reports any problem back to the agent. **Create a task to fix it**, on a broken theme file, starts the same kind of task with that file's problems listed.

#### Themes in a remote window

Themes belong to this computer, as your choice of theme does. Every window, including one connected to a remote environment, lists and installs themes in this computer's themes folder and gallery. In a window connected to another machine, the picker adds an **On {host}** group with that machine's themes, compared with the copies on this computer:

| The theme on {host} | The picker offers |
|---|---|
| Not on this computer | **Install {name} on this computer** |
| A copy you installed from {host} earlier, changed since | **Update {name} from {host}**, which updates it at once |
| A later version of your own copy | **Update {name} to {version} from {host}**, marked **Update to {version}** |
| An earlier version of your own copy | **Replace {name} on this computer with the copy on {host}**, marked **Older than yours** |
| A copy that differs from yours in another way | **Replace {name} on this computer with the copy on {host}**, marked **Differs from yours** |

Updating or replacing your own copy asks first: **Update {name} to {version}?** or **Replace {name} on this computer?**.
